China’s fiscal and monetary policy stances have also been discretionary and determined mainly by each year’s specific economic situation. Historically, only one of the last four FYPs saw an increase in general account fiscal deficit in their initial year (Figure 6). Monetary policy actions were also idiosyncratic in the first year of the last five FYPs: two saw rate hikes while the other three saw no change to policy rates (Figure 7). Specifically for 2021, the starting year of the prior FYP, the authorities kept the policy rate unchanged and scaled back fiscal stimulus to prevent the economy from overheating after the aggressive easing in 2020. For 2026, therefore, we think macro policies and the pace of implementation of the FYP will be determined by whether growth stays in the authorities’ “comfort zone”. records.text: lustrative purposes, we use the FRBUS model to simulate a one-off decline in the 30- year residential mortgage rate by 100bp. Before proceeding to the results, we make three points: 1. This is not to say that we believe $200bn in purchases of agency mortgage- backed securities will lead to a 100bp reduction in the 30-year fixed mortgage rate. It is standard practice in the economic literature to introduce shocks of a reasonable magnitude and readers can scale those effects up or down. For example, if the $200bn in bond purchases reduce the mortgage rate by 25bp, the results below should be divided by four. 2. We think it is better to assume the effect of asset purchases on mortgage yields is temporary as opposed to permanent given that the directive is for a fixed quantity of bond purchases as opposed to a yield target. The exercise can be viewed as the economic effects of temporarily lowering the mortgage rate while bond purchases are executed. 3. We allow for an endogenous response for monetary policy (the FRB/US model embeds a Taylor Rule-like response function for monetary policy). An alternative would be to keep monetary policy unchanged. This turns out to be a distinction without a difference given that the optimal monetary policy response is minor. 1. Looking back in history, policy pivots were usually adopted as part of a crisis management approach. Hypothetically, there could be a set of triggers : ▪ Imminent risks that growth falls below the official target. China’s cumulative growth had fallen to 4.8% in the first three quarters of 2024, which meant a material rebound in Q4 was needed to achieve the 5% full-year target. The subsequent policy pivot did drive growth up to 5.4% y/y in Q4, which resulted in the full-year 5% target being successfully fulfilled . For 2026, whether the growth target is set at 5% once again or lowered to 4.5%, it is a close call. However, we sense that policy acceptance of slower growth has increased. Thus, as in 2024, imminent risks of growth dropping below 4.5% could prompt increased policy response . ▪ Social pressures: The most recent example was the authorities’ sudden exit from the zero-Covid policy in late 2022. For 2026, a more likely trigger on the social front stems from labor market pressures. In hindsight, the decision to adopt the RMB4trn stimulus program in late 2008 was partly based on the report that 20mn migrant workers returned to the countryside after losing their jobs in the cities. With 'Liberation Day' behind us, trade will likely remain front and centre for the UK. A key focus area will be around the UK-EU Trade & Cooperation Agreement (TCA), which will be up for re-evaluation later this year. The UK Government has talked up closer ties with its largest trading partner - including, and in particular, closer alignment with the EU single market. But make no mistake: this won't be a 'Brexit Big Bang 2.0'. From a macro and markets standpoint, expectations should centre around a rolling series of technical negotiating rounds rather than one fixed “cliff-edge” date, with risk clustering around: landing the SPS deal by mid-year, the June 2026 fisheries/energy deadline, and any high-profile UK-EU summit where leaders might package small wins into a “reset 2.0”. The main upside scenario is modest but meaningful friction-reduction in agrifood and some manufactured goods via SPS and customs/rules of origin tweaks. Of course, we stress that we do not have insight into what the DA will present at the grand jury, and it is possible they have evidence of perjury. If that were the case, then the risk of Powell’s exit increases. But even if the grand jury indicts and then the case goes to trial, it could take quarters or years before a resolution. In such a case, the Trump administration could try to remove Powell for cause. But considering that SCOTUS has permitted Lisa Cook to maintain her Fed role as her case progresses (and that SCOTUS in general does seem willing to provide some cover for the Fed – see more in our 2026 FX Outlook), it is possible they will do the same for Powell in this scenario. In addition to this, we have seen Republican Senator Tillis threaten to block any Trump appointees to the Fed until this matter is resolved (CNBC 01/12/25). Recall Tillis is on the Senate Banking Committee. The Senate Banking Committee first approves of any appointees with a simple majority before the broader Senate approval process. records.text: Lower house dissolution and general election timing could also impact BoJ rate hikes December Tokyo CPI (26 December) Politics: Timing of dissolution and general election is key The main political focus is, above all, the timing of the lower house dissolution and general election. The Takaichi administration’s approval rating is extremely high at around 75%, but such ratings are usually highest immediately after a new administration is launched and then clearly tend to decline over time ( Figure 22). This time as well, the dissolution is widely expected to come while approval ratings remain high. In addition, PM Takaichi’s term as president of the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) runs until September 2027, but there will be unified local elections in the spring of 2027. Against this backdrop, in order to avoid a "forced dissolution, " the best scenario for establishing a long-term administration would arguably be to hold the general election within 2026 and secure a single-party majority for the LDP in advance. . Looking at the nine dissolutions since 2000, there was one each from June to September, three in October and two in November. Realistically, the three possible timings for dissolution may be: (1) after passage of the FY26 budget in April or later, (2) just before the end of the regular Diet session in late June, or (3) during the extraordinary Diet session in the autumn. No, we expect it to stabilize. In H2 2025 investment growth plunged to unprecedented lows, driven by the deepening property-sector slump, the anti-involution campaign and tighter fiscal discipline over local-government hidden debt. Some of these headwinds may ease in 2026. Property investment: The 16% decline in property related capital outlays already outpaced the 11% fall in property sale values in 2025. As a lagging indicator, property investment still needs to catch up with the sales contraction (Figure11). Given the gap narrowed in 2025, we anticipate the 2026 decline will ease to roughly 10%. Manufacturing investment: Almost every manufacturing sub-sector — whether traditional or emerging, whether located in the east or west of China — experienced synchronized drops in H2 2025. The anti-involution campaign after President Xi’s meeting on 1 July appears to be the main driver. Two follow-up measures likely curtailed investment : 1) Tighter limits on incentives that local government can offer in terms of cheap land, tax breaks and subsidies to court investment . 2) Stricter approval of new capex projects to curb overcapacity. records.text: 2 Europe Economic Weekly | 09 January 2026 Weekly view Back to school: New Year, same base case We start the year, as usual, with a “back to school” summary and the usual calendar of events (Exhibit 4). Our base case for the Euro area and the UK remains largely unchanged: In the Euro area, we expect 1% growth in 2026 and an acceleration to 1.4% in 2027, masking an improvement in sequential growth as German fiscal stimulus comes through. That’s very close to consensus. We are below consensus on inflation, with headline at 1.6% in 2026 and now also 1.6% in 2027 (-20bp, ETS2 driven). Consequently, we still expect the next ECB move to be a cut in March, followed by a long hold. In the UK, we expect 1.2% growth this year. Recent dataflow suggests zero quarterly growth for 4Q25, so we change our forecasts accordingly, with better 1Q26 prospects. Inflation should fall to 2.2% this year and to 2.0% in 2027, partly due to energy price measures. That’s still compatible with two more BoE cuts in March and June, but we see risks of stickier inflation dynamics and consequently later and/or less BoE cuts. What you may have missed in the Euro area over the break Data flow in the Euro area in December and early January was mixed: Soft data remained lacklustre. Prediction markets favored Hassett in late-fall, but Warsh has gained momentum recently (Figure 4. . . o n l i n e m a r k e t s h a d f a v o r e d H a s s e t t i n t h e f a l l , b u t W a r s h ’ s s t a r h a s b e e n o n t h e r i s e i n t h e n e w y e a r ). President Trump has been very vocal in his desire to lower policy rates and it seems likely he will choose a more dovish candidate, which should keep the OIS curve inverted until the new Chair joins in June. We firmly believe that the Fed Chair’s power to drive policy decisions emanates from their ability to create consensus on the Committee. The latest Summary of Economic Projections, released at the December FOMC meeting, projects just one ease in 2026, and the distribution of the “dots” shows that 7 of 19 Committee members forecast no cuts this year. Thus, even with a strongly dovish FOMC Chair, we believe it’s unlikely a new FOMC Chair will find support for more easing unless labor markets weaken rapidly. If Pow- ell steps down as governor when his term as Fed chair ends in May, then the administration would have two new governors, which is probably not enough to swing the Committee toward more aggressive easing. This significant exposure has raised concerns around widespread and permanent job loss, sparking fears of a “job apocalypse” or “humans going the way of horses.” We expect that the AI transition will lead to a meaningful amount of labor n displacement. Our baseline forecast for a 15% AI-driven labor productivity uplift and the historical relationship between technologically driven productivity gains and job loss implies that 6-7% of jobs will be displaced over the adoption period. Risks are skewed toward greater displacement if AI proves more labor displacing than prior technologies. While increased AI-driven displacement may create significant real income losses n and economic headwinds for affected workers, AI will also create new jobs. AI infrastructure investment is already boosting employment. Productivity gains increase capacity and lower costs, providing an employment tailwind in sectors where demand is not saturated. And technological change is a main driver of long-run job growth via the creation of new occupations—only 40% of workers today are employed in occupations that existed 85 years ago—suggesting that AI will create new roles even as it renders others obsolete. There are several channels through which technological change can create new n kinds of jobs. First, it can create new occupations directly. Productivity growth tends to move in regimes. In the last 75 years, there have been two regimes of ~1.5% and two of ~ 3%. The trend since 2004 appears to have been ~1.6% annualized, with growth of ~1.8% annualized since the onset of the pandemic. While it's impossible to know for sure, in the higher productivity regime of the 1990s investment and capital intensity shifted higher and we may be seeing the start of that now with the increased investment related to AI. In today’s Daily, we launch our Q4 GDP tracking estimate and outline how the backlog of data and the government shutdown have impacted our forecast. We are launching our Q4 GDP tracking estimate at 2.1% (quarter-over-quarter n annualized), 1.1pp above the Bloomberg consensus but 3.0pp below the Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow model. Unlike the Atlanta Fed model, our estimate incorporates a large drag on Q4 GDP growth (-1.1pp) from the government shutdown, primarily as a result of federal employee furloughs. Private domestic final sales growth, which excludes government spending, inventories, and net exports, should provide a better gauge of underlying growth in Q4. records.text: 2 Curating the FX factor zoo: We leverage the wide body of academic and practitioner literature that has documented persistent risk premia in FX. Our factor universe includes the traditional carry, long-term value and momentum signals, as well as extending to more recent discoveries including skewness and fundamental momentum. We also consider alternative construction techniques for traditional factors and include risk factors such as beta to world equities or commodities. Most of our factors are cross-sectional, but we have also included timeseries-based factors (for trend- following or skewness, for instance). Key academic references for FX factors are included on page 25. Our construction methodology is consistent across factors. We opt for simple rules, with no bells or whistles. This could well be improved in future publications by refining the rules for each style, but this simple approach offers robustness benefits. The raw signal data, whether 12-month forward points or discount to purchasing price parity (PPP) fair values for all nine USD pairs, is first transformed into winsorized z-scores (+/- 3). The USD score is a residual of the cross section to fully neutralize scores in the universe. Final factor weights are computed by scaling the transformed signals to a 5% volatility target using a three-month rolling window. We assume a one-day lag between signal computation and trading. Given that tariff rates have varied widely by product and country, we also compute observed trade elasticities this year from product data. We aggregate nominal trade values and changes in static tariff rates by country and by detailed prod- uct, checking both HTS-2 and HTS-4 product aggregation. We first bin the data by the size of the tariff rate change, com- pute the mean tariff change in each bin, weighted by 2024 trade volume, and finally compare that to the aggregate change in imports in each bin. Under either HTS-2 or HTS-4 aggregation, the implied elasticity is -1.2 (Figure 3), or -0.9 if we exclude computers. As an additional check, we regress log import changes against log tariff changes at the individual country/product level, weighted by 2024 import shares. That yields an elasticity of -1.7 overall or -1.0 excluding comput- ers (average of HTS-2 and HTS-4 regressions). The services sector, a key driver of domestic activity, saw its confidence indicator ease marginally but remains near its cyclical high, suggesting that domestic demand continues to strengthen. This view is further supported by an upward revision to the Consumer Confidence Indicator. The most notable development came from the manufacturing sector. Despite ongoing headwinds, manufacturer confidence strengthened, according to the European Commission's survey. This divergence from other indicators is likely driven by improving expectations for the future. Indeed, the index for future production expectations rose, particularly in Germany and Italy, and the order book index also improved. While the sector still faces challenges, this forward-looking optimism suggests conditions may be turning a corner, with a potential fiscal boost from Germany likely to provide further support. We think China’s inflation momentum will remain sluggish this year despite a more favorable base effect and the recent pick-up in core inflation readings . The recent uptick in core CPI can be largely attributed to two factors, in our view: the surge in gold prices and the price distortion caused by the consumer goods trade-in subsidy . China’s gold jewelry price is included in the “Other goods & services” CPI category. Although the NBS does not publish monthly gold jewelry CPI, the broader “Other goods & services” CPI has been moving in tandem with the changes in gold prices (Figure 22). Although this item only accounts for about 4% of core CPI, due to the surge in gold price we estimate it alone contributed 0.7pp of the total 1.2% y/y increase in December ’s core CPI. Moreover, the consumer goods trade-in subsidy program also exaggerated core CPI growth. China expanded the scope and scale of the consumer goods trade-in subsidy in 2025, allowing consumers to receive up to 20% fiscal subsidy in home appliance purchases. records.text: ies point to partial pass-through, with expected increases in final prices well below the statutory rise in the IEPS quota. This reflects a combination of competitive pressures, margin absorption and the high price sensitivity of demand, particularly among lower-income households, where consumption of sugary drinks is more concentrated. Other factors could further dampen the inflation impact: These include product reformulation (lower sugar content), a gradual shift in consumption toward low- or zero-sugar alternatives, and price adjustments staggered over several months rather than a one-time jump in January. Together, we believe these channels suggest that while the IEPS hike will temporarily delay inflation convergence in early 2026, it is unlikely to generate second-round effects or weigh on inflation expectations. Fuel excise taxes, by comparison, play a secondary role in this cycle. While fuel IEPS quotas are updated at the start of the year, the increase is relatively small and consistent with recent patterns. Moreover, the effective pass-through to pump prices remains conditional on global energy prices and the use of fiscal smoothing mechanisms. As a result, fuel-related IEPS adjustments are not the main driver behind our inflation call for early 2026. This may be helping to drive the marginally more hawkish pricing in Fed Funds as well. Market Impact The net effect of the above is actually marginally more hawkish – not dovish, though we stress “marginal” as it is the data that will drive Fed action going forward. Market pricing for the Fed Funds rate through June (which in theory includes the new Chair’s first meeting) has risen to 3.4%, which means we now have less than a full cut priced through that period (Figure 3). This could help explain the more muted USD sell-off overnight as the rates market is effectively saying this should not impact Fed pricing for now (and again may actually be marginally hawkish). Still, the knee-jerk USD response is understandable given the recent USD rally and general concerns around Fed independence as a negative USD driver. However, we think bounces in EURUSD like we saw overnight are an opportunity for shorts. The 1.17-1.1708 area has been pivotal over the past month and should hold as resistance, making risk/reward attractive for shorts here. US CPI on Tuesday is the next catalyst to watch, and we suspect a 0.3 MoM core CPI reading (in line with US Economics and median forecasts) supports the Fed staying on hold in January. Over the past month or two, the Takaichi administration has indicated a desire to avoid JPY weakening toward 160 to the USD, likely due to the US administration’s view that BoJ normalization is effective in correcting JPY depreciation as well as public dissatisfaction with cost-push inflation caused by a weaker JPY. A large increase in the pipeline In its December projections, the Bundesbank predicted a wid- ening of the German government deficit from 2.5% of GDP in 2025 to 4.8% of GDP by 2028, with 2026 already at 3.9% of GDP. The projection for 2026 and 2027 is broadly aligned with our own view and implies a widening of the structural primary deficit of 2% of GDP by 2027. The Bundesbank made these projections despite discussing at length the vari- ous constraints faced by the construction sector and the plan- ning system, and despite arguing that only half of the spend- ing from the Special Fund for infrastructure would be truly “additional”. Our forecast also assumes only a partial delivery in terms of some of the investments. This effect will boost prices for both goods and services – for example, for medical care. In addition, the fact that data collection resumed later in the month of November likely meant that seasonal holiday sales were oversampled relative to past years. This distortion likely biased lower prices for a number of goods that typically see holiday sales, including apparel, home furnishings, and con- sumer electronics. We expect a material further bounce back in the December prices across these various categories. Shelter prices behave slightly differently as a result of the shutdown, owing to the fact that they are collected once every six months in a rotating panel. As October prices were treated as unchanged by the BLS, that means the change from cumu- lative two-month change from September to November more accurately reflects the monthly change for November, and computing the growth rates from interpolated index data should produce a November figure that is roughly half as large as it should be. The impact of skipping the October data collection should continue to bias down the index levels for both owners’ equivalent rent and tenants’ rent until the panel that was supposed to be updated in October gets refreshed next April. records.text: In Ingredients, we explore four thematic ideas and two stock ideas. Following a de-rating in 2025, we examine the potential for share price recovery across the space if Consumer Ingredients volume growth were to return to historical outperformance levels vs. listed Staples, potentially restoring historical premium valuations. We also examine the progress US food companies have delivered on pledges to remove artificial colours and the potential impact if seed oils were to be next in the cross hairs of the MAHA (Make America Healthy Again) movement. Buybacks were a theme in 2025; we highlight scope for and the potential impact of accelerated buybacks in Consumer Ingredients in 2026. In the Salmon space, we recently turned more constructive and also expect more FCF to be returned to shareholders in 2026, but we flag a tail risk of regulatory push towards closed containment farming, which could require higher capex. In terms of individual stocks, we analyse the potential impact on Novonesis from a scenario where Carbios scales r-PET capacity in China to 1m tonnes, which might in theory lead to a potential upward revision of Novonesis’ OSG guide to 2030, and the downside risk if AAK’s CBE margins compress in 2026. In the Ingredients space, our key Overweights are Novonesis (PT DKK470), Kerry (PT €102), and Givaudan (PT CHF3900). We are Underweight on AAK (PT SEK255). As a result, we no longer expect the Fed to ease at the January meeting. If the labor market weakens again in the coming months, or if inflation falls materially, the Fed could still ease later this year. However, we expect the labor market to tighten by the second quarter and the disinflation process to be quite gradual. Consequently, we now expect the Fed to hold rates throughout 2026 with the next move to hike later in 2027. We pencil in one 25bp hike in 3Q27 to bring the (upper band for the) policy rate back up to 4%. Coming into this week, there were already upside risks to our 4Q25 GDP projection of 1.0% before the labor market data, alongside other data out this week, spurred an upgrade. Fol- lowing a sharp contraction in the October trade balance, we’ve raised our 4Q25 GDP forecast to 2.5%, though absent the government shutdown it would be closer to 3%. records.text: Japan Macro Watch9 January 2026 ab 2 2026 benign outlook with potential risks Incoming data for October and November showed that our Q4 GDP forecast was too conservative. As shown on Page 9, monthly data on consumption, exports and imports of goods and services, and public investment suggest that these demand components rose more than we had expected. We thus now expect Q4 GDP to rise close to 2% q/q, saar after a -2.3% contraction in Q3, instead of a more modest 1% rise. Our CY2026 GDP growth forecast looks for 1.1% YoY after 1.2% in 2025, but we see the momentum of growth strengthening. Indeed, our FY2026 (starting in April) growth forecast anticipates 1.2% growth after 1.0% in FY2025 (ending March 2026). Our near- term growth forecast is somewhat higher than the market consensus (Figure 1) as our assessment on impact of the fiscal package introduced at end of last year is stronger than the consensus view. The economic outlook for 2026 is positive, supported by three tailwinds. First, the global economic outlook is favorable. While we think real GDP growth likely slowed in Q4 after registering very strong (4.3% q/q saar) growth in the prior quarter, we expect it to have remained resilient, supported by consumer spending, business fixed investment, and net exports. On inflation, we expect monthly prints to remain elevated in coming months. While the November CPI print came in significantly below expectations, we think the surprise largely reflected distortions related to the lack of data collection in October and early November due to the government shutdown. We expect these distortions to be unwound in coming months, with the December, January, and April CPI prints incorporating upward biases that should offset the downward bias of 20-25bp estimated for the November %m/m core CPI. Our forecast has monthly core CPI inflation printing at 0.35% m/m in December, 0.50% m/m in January and 0.32% m/m in April, with the latter capturing the unwind of the distortion to rents/OER. While biases to the PCE measures of inflation are likely to be smaller than those for the CPI, and the FOMC will likely want to look through these distortions, an acceleration in core PCE in coming months would make it difficult for FOMC participants to gain confidence that inflation is reverting to the 2% objective. We think the committee will want to see evidence that m/m inflation has peaked before cutting rates again.

Prior to the war in Ukraine, Russia was a key supplier of wood to the Finnish P&P industry. The closure of that supply has led to elevated wood costs for the downstream Finnish P&P industry (however, as discussed above, costs are now coming down). Most of the Finnish downstream P&P is currently operating at break-even levels and is unviable, as is evident from the recent results of UPM and Stora if one removes the highly profitable LatAm operations of these companies. It is also evident in the results of Metsa Board, which has reported -ve EBIT margins for a few quarters. A resumption of Russian wood supply – even if it were to occur in FY26/27 – would be likely to lead to further lower wood costs in Finland and Scandinavia, and boost the profitability of the downstream operations of both Stora and UPM. We estimate the current stock prices assume that the Finnish downstream operations remain break-even in perpetuity. We don't agree that this will be the case. Potential impact on stocks The upside for Stora and UPM appears potentially quite significant, and more for Stora than for UPM, in our view. Given that there is no concrete pathway to a resolution yet, we haven't undertaken a detailed scenario analysis. However, to illustrate the potential impact, we use Stora Enso as an example.

After a sharp hawkish repricing, Australia now boasts the highest yields in the G10, a status that should attract flows and unwind long-held shorts. A fall in goods exports drove the narrowing, down -2.9%M, driven by a large fall in metal ores (- 9.1%M). Rural exports were stronger (+9.6%M). Gold exports fell in the month, however annual growth remains strong (~46%Y). Gold imports unwound following October's surge (-11%M vs +80%M prev). A softer print driven by softer exports. Nevertheless we continue to watch for growth in capital goods imports as a signal of rising domestic capex intentions. records.text: TRADE IDEA T R A D EI D E A 09/01/2026 1 We initiated two trades on 11 December 2025 aiming to monetise a seasonal pattern of investors positioning for year- ahead trades in the old year’s final two weeks and the first week of the new year. These were long a consensus trades basket by consensus year-ahead forecast return (long AUD, SEK, NOK; short EUR, CHF, USD) and short the DXY, with consensus bearish the USD for the year-ahead. With today marking the end of the period when consensus trades historically perform well, we exit these positions. We book a small gain on the consensus trades basket and a minor loss on the short DXY trade for a combined small gain. The long/short basket displayed a similar pattern to history, but returns troughed later and peaked earlier than was the case previously (Figure 1). We therefore missed out on the positive returns from the market allocating to these trades. Looking ahead, our backtest shows consensus trades typically work for only a short time in January. As a result, our bias is to be nimble and fade these trades where positioning and valuations are stretched. Our metrics show that positioning is notably pronounced in consensus longs (AUD, SEK, NOK), which suggests that these currencies could be particularly liable to a reversal. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 409/01/2026 US–China rate differential vs FX settlement (goods) ratio Rolling sum of exporters' under-settled positions since 2020 Exporters’ FX settlement picked up in 2025Q4: How will corporates’ FX settlement strategy change? Corporates’ FX settlement ratios have fluctuated significantly over time. Before the 2015 exchange-rate reform, exporters had expected a one-way RMB appreciation, and their settlement ratio was very high (sometimes >100%). After the reform, the settlement ratio has steadily declined. Chinese corporates were hit hard during the 2018–19 China–US trade war, China’s Covid- 19 period and the latest round of housing-deleveraging concerns. The downtrend in the settlement ratio was largely consistent with the trend in spot FX and rate differential. However, the settlement ratio recovered occasionally when the DXY fell, for instance in 2017 and 2021. More recently in Q4 2022 and H2 2025, we observe quarterly recovery in corporate activities when the USD and USD yields corrected lower. We estimate how much exporters’ settlements have deviated from average by using the 12-month moving average settlement ratio as a baseline and calculating each month’s deviation from that average. This approach shows that exporters’ accumulated under-settled positions have fallen from the peak of about USD204bn in May 2022 to roughly USD109.7bn as at November 2025

records.text: 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa Distributed on: 12/01/2026 11:59:05 GMT Distributed on: 12/01/2026 11:59:05 GMT 12 January 2026 Deutsche Bank Research Europe United Kingdom Economics UK economic notes Date After a disappointing start to the fourth quarter, we expect some rebound in November. Some catch-up in activity, we think, is likely. Activity trackers improved in November, as Budget uncertainty diminished. We will also be looking for any (upward) revisions to either the September or October GDP prints. What do we expect for November? We expect GDP to have expanded – albeit marginally. Our models point to a 0.1% m-o-m expansion. Our backcast also points to some meaningful chance of upward revisions to September/October GDP – which came in unexpectedly weaker than our modelled estimates. Looking ahead, we expect GDP to rebound strongly in Q1-26. Survey data are already improving as the dust on the Budget settles. And there are tentative signs that the labour market may be stabilising. We expect households to spend a little more to start the year, and investment to remain on an uptrend (for both the public and private sectors). Base effects, however, will mean that GDP growth this year will be a little lower than in 2025 (1.1%), but we expect quarterly growth to be tracking at a healthy 0.35% q-o-q. Exhibit 1 shows the 100 exogenous initial decline in the residential mortgage rate, which then gradually returns to its prior value over serval quarters. This simulation suggests that growth in real GDP rises by about 0.1-0.15pp after three quarters and the unemployment rate falls by about 0.05pp (half a tenth). The decline in mortgage rates produces a minimal boost to inflation, a trivial increase in the 10y US Treasury yield, and a 5-6bp increase in the federal funds rate. On net, the results of the simulation look like a (very small) aggregate demand shock. One reason for the minimal economic effect is that the drop in the mortgage rate happens in isolation; other interest rates in the model remain unchanged and only adjust in response to changes in activity, inflation, and monetary policy as a result of the drop in mortgage rates. This could include removal of the 10% Fentanyl tariffs against China (e.g., during President Trump’s scheduled visit to China in April) and renegotiation of the USMCA. If the tariffs are struck down, the economy should benefit from an easier fiscal stance (wider deficit), though the tailwind will be partially offset by another bout of trade uncertainty. This scenario should be slightly disinflationary in the near-term. Retailers who have already passed the tariffs through might hold off on additional price hikes for an extended period (they might even lower some prices). Those that have absorbed the tariffs so far would also have less reason to raise prices going forward. This might make it easier for the Fed to cut rates a little further by assuaging the hawks on the FOMC who are concerned about inflation persistence. But we’d expect the impact on monetary policy to be limited, given that i) the majority of the committee is willing to look through the impact of tariffs on inflation, and ii) an easier fiscal stance could stimulate demand, creating upside risks to inflation down the line.

Looking at the probability distribution of the terminal rate calculated from the 2y forward 3m swaptions, since the end of November there has been a clear rightward shift (an upward revision in rate levels) and an increase in dispersion (heightened uncertainty; Figure 7). Even at the BoJ meeting in December, there was no communication regarding the specific level of the terminal rate, leaving uncertainty elevated. Uncertainty around the terminal rate stems from JPY depreciation and the monetary policy cycle of overseas central banks. As the BoJ hikes have so far failed to meaningfully reverse JPY depreciation, the BoJ has indicated a stance of hiking in response to JPY weakness and the markets have started to price a higher and wider distribution for the terminal rate. However, we believe the main driver of USDJPY shifted from rate differentials to equities (US AI/ digital exceptionalism narrative) in 2024, indicating that meaningful JPY appreciation is hard to expect based on BoJ hikes alone (see An AI revolution for the dollar - the (AI)lephant in the room). Yet, any halt to the hiking cycle would increase the risk of further JPY depreciation, so market expectations for rate hikes are likely to remain entrenched. Election is a binary risk: Hungary’s election, due in April 2026, is likely to generate considerable market volatility – not least because we expect a binary market reaction to the outcome. Most opinion polls show the opposition Tisza party leading by as much as 10pp. However, winning the popular vote may still fail to secure a majority as a recent overhaul to the electoral system seems to favour the ruling Fidesz party. A victory for the pro-EU Tisza party could improve access to EU funds and reduce the domestic risk premium, which should help tighten the ASW. In any case, we are minded to go long the ASW into any widening after the election as we go into the windfall tax season in Q4, which should see local banks resuming bond purchases.

records.text: US Economics Weekly9 January 2026 ab 32 Tax season tracking The One Big Beautiful Bill Act implemented tax changes retroactive to 2025. That means individuals can claim refunds against their 2025 income when they file their 2025 tax returns in 2026. Because the tax law changes were passed midyear, most individuals were unlikely to fully account for the changes by adjusting their withheld income. As a result, we expect larger than normal tax refunds sent to households in 2026. We have seen a range of estimates for how strong the refund season might be this spring, from as low as $30 billion more than 2025 to as high as $100 billion. We suspect there may be other estimates even higher. We estimate refund checks to households $50 to $60 billion higher this year than last year. That could be right or wrong, but this is something we can track in real time from the Daily Treasury Statement. As shown in the two figures below, we can trace out the magnitude of refunds flowing out of the Treasury Department to households. We can also track how changes in withholding tables might be leaving more money in workers' pockets too. To the extent refunds are exceeding last year, or disappointing expectations, this can be assessed in close to real time. We are just starting out the year and the individual tax filing season formally begins the last week of January with the deadline for filing being April 15, "Tax Day". records.text: 6 Global Economic Weekly | 09 January 2026 Why are tariff revenues undershooting? It is also worth noting that IEEPA-related tariff collection has been less than expected: this reduces the impact of a Supreme Court ruling in either direction. Yesterday’s trade data indicate an effective tariff rate of 11.2% in November 2025 (per the usual, we assume tariffs collected in November correspond to October imports). The effective rate has stabilized around this level for three months, and might even decline for November imports based on Daily Treasury Statements for December (Exhibit 2). This contradicts our prior expectation that it would move up significantly further once the measures announced over the summer were fully reflected in the data (which should be the case by now). There are two reasons for the undershoot in tariff collection. First, importers have substituted away from high-tariff products/countries to a considerable degree. We estimate that this substitution has reduced the effective tariff rate by around 3pp. Based on the measures that have been announced, the mix of imports as of Oct 2025 should (per our calculations) have resulted in an average tariff rate of 14.5%. The corresponding figures for Oct 2023 and Oct 2024 are around 17.5%. records.text: US Economic Weekly | 09 January 2026 9 Core views Growth: a dose of optimism • We remain constructive on the US economy. Inflation: to remain stuck above the Fed’s target through 2027 • We continue to expect inflation to remain above the Fed's target throughout our forecast horizon. In the near term, supply-driven inflation due to tariffs should push inflation above 3% y/y through 3Q 2026 as businesses continue to slowly shift costs to consumers. Inflationary pressures from tariffs should fade towards the end of 2026; however, core PCE inflation should end 2026 at an elevated 2.9% y/y and only decline to 2.4% by year end 2027. We continue to believe underlying inflation is above 2%, and our growth and monetary policy outlook should generate more demand driven inflation causing a delay in inflation’s return to the Fed’s 2% target. While the growth drag from US tariffs should recede this year, we expect a continued headwind from Chinese export competition, to which Germany is particularly exposed. German manufacturing activity has stabilised after several years of decline. We n expect a slow recovery as domestic demand improves but Germany continues to lose global market share. The labour market should improve gradually as growth picks up, with unemployment falling towards the natural rate. While there has been some limited progress—for example, on investment incentives, planning and permitting— more meaningful reforms are still lacking. records.text: M Update 2 December Employment The Canadian economy added 8.2k jobs in December, driven by healthcare and construction, while professional services were a large drag. Unemployment rate rose to 6.83% (+0.29pp) while participation rate rose to 65.36% (+0.22pp). Year-over-year population growth decelerated to 1.28% (-0.15pp). • Full-time employment rose by 50.2k while part-time employment fell by 42.0k, a reversal from the past two months. • Services sector employment was flat at the headline, with considerable changes at an industry level. Over the three preceding months, the services sector had added 128.8k jobs, and has accounted for 207k of the 226k jobs added by the Canadian economy in 2025. ° The healthcare sector added 21k jobs, and has added 85k jobs this year. ° The trade sector lost 5.6k jobs, but has added nearly 50k jobs this year, despite being highly exposed to trade-related uncertainty facing the economy. ° Professional services lost 18k jobs in December, with flat employment this year. ° Education, Information services and transport have added 5-15k jobs this year, with volatile monthly prints. Other sectors added ~40k jobs. • Goods-producing industries added ~8k of the 8.2k jobs added this year, and have added 19k jobs this year. AI’s Impact on Unemployment While we are optimistic that AI will create new jobs that absorb displaced workers, finding a job takes time, particularly if workers need to reskill to transition to new industries. As a result, we expect a notable increase in “frictional” unemployment that raises the unemployment rate even under our optimistic view regarding AI’s labor market impacts. How much could the unemployment rate rise as displaced workers are transitioning to new roles? Under our baseline assumptions that 1) the adoption timeline is 10 years at the firm level (with 6-year intra-firm adoption lags), 2) 6-7% of workers are displaced during this transition period, and 3) most workers take less than a year to find a new job (more specifically, we assume that most workers find new jobs at a rate consistent with the unemployment rate impulse shown in Exhibit 3), we estimate a peak gross unemployment rate increase of around 0.6pp (corresponding to a 1mn increase in unemployed workers; Exhibit 10). Given emerging evidence that AI (when appropriately deployed) can deliver significant efficiency gains, recent corporate commentary suggesting that AI automation raises the bar for hiring for new roles, and survey responses from our GS banking team pointing to AI-driven headcount reductions among large US corporates over the next 1-3 years, we anticipate that widespread adoption of AI will lead to meaningful labor displacement. Combining our baseline forecast for a 15% AI-driven labor productivity uplift with the historical relationship between technological-driven productivity gains and job loss (left chart, Exhibit 3) implies that 6-7% of jobs could be displaced as AI is widely adopted. This estimate corresponds to AI fully automating work in the 20-30% most exposed occupations (ranked by the AI-displacement risk scores that we developed last year). If AI proves more labor-displacing than historical technologies, the overall displacement rate would be higher (right chart, Exhibit 3). We expect supply additions to accelerate in 2027-28, pushing JKM prices another ~25% below futures & stimulating price-sensitive demand. Oversupply in the global LNG market is also bearish for European gas prices, which we see falling back to €20/MWh by 2028. Metals: Upside Ahead: We keep a positive skew to our metals outlook, supported by rate cuts and demand for real assets, while low inventories and tightening balances drive price upside. We are above consensus for almost all metals in 2026. Our top picks are uranium and lithium, we still see upside to gold, copper, and aluminum, and are more cautious on iron ore and zinc. The closer they get, the harder it is to find agreement on whether rates should move, and data dependency will be key. records.text: void seed oils. Consumer concerns over seed oils have moved into the mainstream, prompting major food brands to reformulate products and adjust sourcing. Sweetgreen launched its first “seed oil-free menu, ” while Roots Farm Fresh eliminated seed oils entirely to meet health-conscious demand. The Corn Refiners Association and the National Oilseed Processors Association have rebuked concerns about seed oils. In collaboration with the Barclays Data Science team, our analysis of ingredient lists across approximately 34K food and beverage products from Walmart and Albertsons reveals that rapeseed oil (14% penetration), soybean oil (14%), and sunflower oil (10%) are the most prevalent among the eight oils assessed. Additionally, the data indicates that over 50% of bakery and snack products contain one or more oils in their ingredients, followed by confectionery at around 30%. Beverages, on the other hand, remain largely unaffected and pose minimal risk from any potential seed oil regulations. Seed oils account for around 20% of AAK’s raw material volumes. In our view, potential regulation or stepped-up MAHA pressure to reduced seed oil usage could pose the greatest potential headwind for AAK within our coverage universe. 9 January 2026 28 Barclays | European Materials

Our bullish USDJPY view is based on domestic and global factors. On the domestic front, the new administration’s expansionary fiscal policies and dovish monetary policy bias should continue to weigh on the currency, while verbal interventions so far indicate that any eventual action may still be steps away. In addition, the JPY may face further selling pressures due to its correlation to the JGB term premia, particularly if Takaichi decides to call for an early snap election that strengthens her political mandate to pursue more expansionary economic policies (see the JPY part of the overview). On the global front, US exceptionalism is a triple whammy for the JPY: 1) the decline in global equity risk premia has reduced safe-haven demand for the JPY, especially since 2023; 2) capital flows from Japan to the US equity persist, including retail flows under the New NISA tax exemption scheme; and 3) " digital deficits" continue to grow. Monetary policy (last updated 19 December) Amid JPY depreciation pressures toward 160 to the USD and given the alleviation of risk originating from the US and reduced uncertainty around tariffs, the BoJ decided on a rate hike to 0.75% at its December meeting (the first such move since January, nearly a year ago). As for the momentum of the 2026 spring wage negotiations, which has been viewed as a key factor for rate hikes, the Bank explained that it was able to collect the necessary information from corporate hearings earlier than usual this year. Since 0.75% is a policy rate level not seen in 30 years, any subsequent rate hike to 1% will likely be approached cautiously, with careful monitoring of the impact on economic activity over time. In this sense, it would arguably be ideal to confirm the momentum of 2027 wage negotiations before making the next hike. However, given the strengthening concern about JPY depreciation, both within the Takaichi administration and at the BoJ, it may be difficult to stand pat for a prolonged period, suggesting the the BoJ could return to its previous hiking pace of once per six months. We used web-scraped data for a total of ~34k products from the Walmart and Albertsons online grocery stores, collecting information on ingredients as well as other information such as price. This raw data from two of the largest US food retailers allowed us to gather granular ingredient and product pricing intelligence of products across the food and beverage categories. We used basic NLP techniques (e.g. regular expressions) to process the ingredients of each of the products to identify their frequency and bucket artificial and natural colours' product penetration across product sub-categories. Our proprietary web scraping analysis indicated c21% penetration of artificial colours, similar to one of the recent studies by lead study author Dr. Elizabeth Dunford, which indicated 19%. Interestingly there has been no change in the aggregate penetration, but we find that penetration has come down in confectionery and bakery and snacks. FIGURE 43. This, in turn, helps identify this adjustment process using fitted models. As the market rent indicator for our models, we use Zillow Observed Rent Index (ZORI). Although this index suffers from the same shortcoming as other market rent indicators because its repeat-rent methodology is limited to new leases, we prefer it amongst other alternatives because of its broad coverage, which draws from a dataset that includes more than 100mn US housing units throughout the US, using weights calibrated to be representative of the overall US rental housing stock.5 We also like ZORI because it is available at the same frequency as the CPI (monthly), can be expressed as a level index, and because it is less volatile than competing private sector indices. (The appendix applies our methodology to the REIS index, a market rent indicator for multifamily units that is available at a quarterly frequency.) records.text: 2 Japan Viewpoint | 09 January 2026 Big picture: Minor expansion of government spending The fiscal debates that had been ongoing since the start of the Takaichi administration in October 2025 reached a key milestone at the tail end of 2025. Following the FY25 supplementary budget passed by the Diet on 16 December (see New stimulus under the new PM’s expansionary fiscal stance, 21 November 2025), the government announced its FY26 tax reform blueprint on 19th and the Cabinet approved its initial FY26 budget proposal on 26th (see What you missed while you were away, 5 January). In big-picture terms, compared with the significant YoY increase in the FY25 supplementary budget, the FY26 tax reforms and initial budget do not appreciably raise fiscal spending. We see this as a signal that the government has taken on board the market’s concerns that major tax cuts and spending increases would weaken fiscal discipline. While we therefore think these measures will do little to stimulate consumer spending, we expect Japan's fiscal deficit to remain well smaller than other major developed economies in 2026 (see Year Ahead 2026: Steady growth, gradual rate hikes , 26 November 2025). In the event that peace is achieved in Ukraine, there is a significant amount of rebuild work which will be required to repair the damage inflicted by the war with Russia. Indeed, the latest Ukraine Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA4) by the World Bank and partners estimates recovery needs at $524bn (over 2.8x GDP , an increase of 8% on the prior year) as of end-2024. Around 13% of housing stock and >8,800 km of major roads have been damaged or destroyed, with these numbers likely to increase given ongoing conflict. Rebuilding will be highly commodity-intensive, particularly in steel and cement for housing and infrastructure. We estimate heavy material-intensive construction costs at $240–260bn, based on RDNA4’s ~$220bn figure for housing, infrastructure, and commercial rebuild as of YE 2024, adjusted by a 15% YoY increase (in line with the observed increases between RDNAs 1-3) to reflect continued fighting through YE 2025. 9 January 2026 73 Barclays | European Materials

A potential tail risk to this positive FCF outlook could arise if there was regulatory momentum towards closed containment farming systems. What are closed contained salmon farms? Traditional open-net pen salmon farming uses large mesh cages anchored in coastal waters, relying on natural water flow. While this approach is cost-efficient and widely adopted, it can expose fish to parasites, disease transmission, and environmental risks, such as waste build-up, and escapes that threaten wild populations. In contrast, closed containment systems – typically land-based or floating tanks – provide a controlled environment with recirculated and filtered water, reducing disease risk, preventing escapes, and enabling waste treatment. Our test also examined whether daily or weekly data yielded better results and evaluated which lookback window performed most effectively (see Estimating the correlation matrix in systematic portfolios, dated 23 September 2025). Assuming half of the margin uplift was driven by spot contracts, we estimate a cyclical tailwind of c30bps attributable to spot sales. To assess the potential impact if cocoa butter prices normalise, we model two scenarios: (1) a 50% unwind of the spot contract margin, which would result in an estimated 3.5% headwind to EBIT , and (2) a full 100% unwind, implying a 7% EBIT headwind. These scenarios highlight the sensitivity of AAK’s profitability to cocoa butter price movements and underscore the importance of monitoring pricing dynamics closely. The BoJ raised rates by 25bp at its December meeting, as widely expected. While Governor Ueda did not specify a neutral rate level, he clarified that previous rate hikes have not produced a strong tightening effect and that several Policy Board members noted the possibility that the recent JPY depreciation could be passed on to import prices. Furthermore, hawkish remarks stood out in the summary of opinions of that meeting. records.text: Over the longer-run, AI-driven productivity gains may directly boost labor demand for some existing services if increased capacity leads to market expansion (see Bessen 2018 for a detailed analysis of this dynamic historically). As shown in Exhibit 5, productivity gains in cotton, steel, and motor vehicle production drove job growth over extended periods as technology-driven capacity increases and cost declines created new demand for these products. Only after demand was saturated did further increases in productivity lead to job losses (although losses were admittedly severe in these industries once this occurred). In the current context, this dynamic suggests that employment in highly-exposed but fast-growing industries (e.g., healthcare) could actually experience an AI hiring tailwind. Most importantly, technological change has been a main driver of employment growth via the creation of new occupations. Exhibit 6 summarizes recent research from David Autor and coauthors that shows how important this force has been both over the long-run. Using data from the Census Bureau’s Alphabetical Indexes of Industries and Occupations, they find that 60% of workers today are employed in occupations that did not exist in 1940. This means that over 85% of the job gains over the last 85 years have accrued to new occupations, most of which were created by technology. records.text: Caroline Coughlin Michael Metcalfe 12 January 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General The US i nflation narrative’s nine lives, a Dec surprise? State Street PriceStats recorded a 4bps fall in December, marking the softest monthly inflation since September 2024 and pushing the annual rate back to 2.7%. This softness mainly reflects lower gas prices, with transportation falling over a full percentage point, partially offset by a robust rise in apparel prices, while other sectors remained seasonally benign (Fig 1). Our central estimates for December’s official release, though still affected by October’s official data gap, point to a 0.26% rise in headline CPI and 0.23% in core CPI (sa)—the latter once again is just below Bloomberg consensus. Over the past year, economists’ consensus for core CPI has been stuck at 0.3% mom, even though there have been eight downside surprises and only one upside. We have been on the right side of the consensus on seven occasions, but consensus forecasters have largely viewed dips below 0.3% to be transitory. December 2025 is no different, though there’s a wider range of estimates this month. The modest 15.9bps (sa) rise in core CPI between Sep-Nov, the smallest two-month gain since the pandemic, is perhaps the biggest test of the idea of mean reversion yet. records.text: mestic automakers. Accompanying this was a sharp decline (45%) in auto import volume during 2022–25 (Figure 21). Contrary to falling imports, China replaced Japan as the world’s biggest auto exporter in 2023. Another sector feeling the consumer shift from buying foreign brands to buying local is cosmetics, whose import value has fallen by nearly 30% from 2022, as great value- for-money local products look more appealing to Chinese customers amid tepid consumer confidence. One sector to witness a significant rise (nearly 70%) in imports has been semiconductors, which now represents 16.3% of China’s total imports, surpassing oil (Figure 18). However, there is a clear ongoing campaign for domestic substitution, and Chinese companies have made impressive strides in enhancing self-sufficiency. So, over time, the degree of import reliance is likely to fall, in our view. With no signs of the trend of domestic substitution reversing, a weak outlook for domestic demand, and the prospect of further declines in global oil prices, we expect China’s imports to continue to stagnate in 2026. This reinforced RMB strength, explaining why USDRMB did not rebound along with DXY. A lack of clear defensive action from the People’s Bank of China (PBoC) in the year end may have also heightened exporters’ concerns that the RMB’s appreciation could persist, prompting additional settlements. The PBoC has continued to deliver lower fixings, instead of setting a flat fixing or having state banks intervene to curb excessive spot movements. Consequently, we saw a relatively swift, one-way RMB appreciation at the end of the year. The PBoC has adjusted the fixing slightly higher later this week to smooth the December one-sided appreciation amid a higher DXY, we think the PBoC may intend to lead the USDRMB higher to prompt further exporter settlement before the Chinese New Year. As such, we still expect this round of RMB appreciation to last into January and may fade before the Chinese New Year. Afterwards, the RMB exchange rate may be more dependent on external factors. Also, looking back at the two rounds of appreciation in April-May and August-September 2025, the USDRMB — after a short-term relatively rapid appreciation — tends to trade sideways and stabilize for a while. No, we don’t think it will lead to a pick-up in growth. The Five-Year Plan (FYP), as its name suggests, is a mid-to-long term roadmap that addresses multiple -year development targets rather than short-term economic issues. We therefore think the pace of implementation of FYP projects will be discretionary, depending on the policy priorities of that year and the position of China’s economy in respective economic cycles, rather than based on the FYP roadmap alone . Evidence supporting this argument is in the lack of a clear pattern of growth and investments in the first year of a FYP. As Figure 4 shows, the economic performance in the first year of the last four FYPs was markedly different: two (2006 and 2021) experienced a rebound in growth, while the others (2011 and 2016) saw growth ease. Crucially, none witnessed a rebound in infrastructure fixed asset investment (FAI) growth (Figure 5), which suggests infrastructure endeavors tend to wane rather than ramp up in the first year of a FYP. records.text: ring expected returns in FX hedging: Investors often exclude expected return assumptions from their mean variance optimization when determining optimal FX hedging ratios. This conservative approach can be consistent with strict risk management, given the challenges of forecasting FX moves. But over the long run, it risks ignoring persistent FX risk premia and therefore underestimating the costs of FX hedging equity portfolios. This may be suboptimal when considering risk- adjusted performance metrics as a yardstick of success. Leveraging on recent practitioners’ research, we propose using a multi-factor framework to inform the return side of the equation in hedging FX risk of equity portfolios. We start with the G10 FX and equity universe, but a similar framework is easily replicable in emerging markets. A second publication on this topic will consider a wider range of techniques to model the equity-FX co- dependence. The bars present the average Sharpe ratio of the full matrix (G10 base currencies investing in G10 local currency equity markets) under various foreign exchange hedging frameworks. The seasonal factors look to have been relatively adaptive to this shift. Upside risks to headline CPI High-frequency inflation data through the end of December indicate that the headline CPI is set to rise 2.5% m/m (data to be released next Tuesday), sticky from the prior month and up from 2.4% on a three-month moving average. We flag upside risks to our forecast, following the release of City of BA CPI at 2.7%m/m. The uptick is expected to be primarily driven by food (+2.5%m/m), especially meat (+7.3%m/m), with beef prices leading the way (+9.6%m/m). The increase in meat prices is expected to more than offset the deflation observed in fresh vegetables (-8.3%m/m). Meanwhile, regulated prices are expected to remain elevated at 2.8% m/m, reflecting adjustments in electricity and gas tariffs, as well as higher transportation and fuel costs. Conversely, core CPI is projected to increase by 3.0% m/m, following November’s acceleration to 2.6% m/m, with risks skewed to the upside following the FX volatility observed in 2H December. Our preferred measure of underlying inflation, core ex food, has accelerated to 2.6%, the highest print since April, and standing above the three-month moving average (2.4%). By component, transportation costs are set to accelerate to 3.8% m/m, driven mainly by higher fuel prices (+7.2% m/m) and increased tariffs (+4.1% m/m). Naive Risk Parity: Within the carry cluster, signals capturing nominal carry, cross-sectional skew and cross-currency basis are equally weighted. The trend cluster combines time-series and cross-sectional trend signals using equal weights. We incorporate additional FX signals, including PPP valuation, time-series skew, the BNP Paribas STEERTM model, relative equity performance and positioning. All signals are combined using inverse volatility weighting and subsequently scaled to a 5% annualised volatility target. MVO with Gerber correlation: As an alternative to the naïve mixing framework, we construct a mean-variance optimized FX portfolio using a rolling one-year Gerber covariance matrix. At each rebalancing date, portfolio weights are obtained by maximising the Sharpe ratio, subject to full investment and no-short-selling constraints. Expected returns in the optimization are estimated using a rolling five-year historical mean. The optimized portfolio is subsequently scaled to a 5% annualised volatility target. We employ the Gerber correlation estimator as it delivers the most stable correlations (page 24). In addition, some affected goods may be held in inventory when tariffs enter into force, which would help to delay and smooth the inflationary impact over time rather than trigger an immediate repricing. Corporate pricing power remains constrained: Importers may absorb part of the cost increase through margins, particularly in highly competitive segments. Re- routing of trade toward countries with which Mexico has preferential agreements (such as Vietnam, Malaysia or Singapore) could further dilute the effective tariff burden. Moreover, the share of value added originating in China varies significantly across consumption categories (for example, it is close to 32% in textiles and apparel but only 8.2% in paper and cardboard, according to the OECD), limiting the scope for a generalized CPI response. Finally, while indirect effects through producer prices cannot be ruled out, these are likely to be gradual and sector-specific. Tariffs on intermediate inputs may raise production costs in sectors such as construction (steel) or manufacturing (aluminum), but for inflation accounting purposes, these effects are better interpreted as cost pressures rather than direct tax shocks. Almost certainly, the FOMC will main- tain an easing bias in January as it emphasizes its inflation optimism and lingering concern that labor market insecurity will undermine households’ willingness to smooth. The real- ization of our recoupling baseline will, however, prompt a more prolonged Fed pause as a rebound in job growth is expected to push the US unemployment rate back to 4.2% this year. There is still a case for disinflation to be a driver of further easing this year, against the backdrop of a dovish shift in Fed leadership. We note, however, that it will take time to see the underlying inflation trajectory, as the unwinding of distortions related to data sampling during the shutdown will linger into 2Q26. Next week’s December CPI report should kick off a run of high-side core CPI readings. Starting with an anticipated 0.4% m/m increase next week, we look for core CPI to increase at a faster than 3% pace in the year ending in May (Figure 3). Against this anticipated macro backdrop, we do not see the new dovish Fed chair being able to sway the FOMC to cut.

records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 309/01/2026 The industrial protection programme approved last year, aimed at strengthening Mexico’s strategic industries and substituting imports from Asia with domestic production. According to the Ministry of Economy, the design of the package sought to limit inflationary pressures. In quantitative terms, the tariffs apply to around 8.6% of total Mexican imports and affect countries without a free trade agreement with Mexico, primarily China. Tariff impact on 2026 inflation could be close to 12bp: The headline tariff increase appears sizable, with average rates rising from around 18% to 30% and automotive duties moving to 50%. However, we consider any transmission to consumer inflation is likely to remain contained. Not all tariff increases will affect final consumer prices: Of the roughly 1,483 tariff lines affected, about 51% correspond to intermediate or industrial-use goods (such as steel, aluminum, textiles, glass and trailers). These products are not directly included in the CPI basket, limiting their immediate mechanical impact on headline inflation. As a result, a significant share of the tariff shock is absorbed upstream in the production chain. We gain exposure to this tactically against HUF which could see volatility around the election in April, and which looks somewhat rich to the deterioration in the public finances (Figure 49). The NBH also sounded dovish in December, and we think could cut rates early this year. The CHF, for the reasons outlined in our colleagues' piece, we believe is another attractive way to be exposed to the crown. We don't have an active trade on the zloty as, while we expect ongoing EU fund flows and growth to be supportive, Poland's current account has deteriorated and the NBP retains on an easing bias for now. Zloty strength could take hold more towards the second half of the year. Short USD/ILS. We remain constructive on the shekel. The global focus on tech and defence plays to the country's comparative advantage in exports and should keep the current account surplus supported. The growth outlook is very positive this year, with demand recovering from the conflict in Gaza and this should restrain the BoI from cutting too deeply despite subdued inflation. records.text: Launching Our Q4 GDP Tracking Estimate The advance reading for Q4 GDP has been delayed from its originally scheduled release date of January 29 due to the government shutdown and is now scheduled for February 20. In today’s Daily, we launch our Q4 GDP tracking estimate and outline how the backlog of data and the government shutdown have impacted our forecast. We are launching our Q4 GDP tracking estimate at 2.1% (quarter-over-quarter annualized), 1.1pp above the Bloomberg consensus but 3.0pp below the Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow model. As we discuss in greater detail below, our forecast incorporates a large drag (-1.1pp) from the government shutdown, but since the Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow model is a nowcast based on available data for the quarter, it cannot anticipate the impact of the shutdown before it materializes in the source data. This accounts for about a third of the gap between our forecast and the GDPNow model. Exhibit 1 shows that adjusting the GDPNow forecast to incorporate our government spending forecast lowers its estimate by 1.4pp to +3.7%. Private domestic final sales growth, which excludes government spending, inventories, and net exports (and therefore will mostly look through the temporary impact of the shutdown), should provide a better gauge of underlying growth in Q4. Based on clinker emissions improvements since the 2016/17 benchmark and recent site closures, we estimate the new benchmark at ~0.65t CO₂/t grey clinker versus 0.693 today—a 1.3% annual decline. With free allocations currently elevated due to weak volumes, we expect an ~8.5% cut in 2026, implying ~5% price upside. By 2030, allowances could halve, potentially driving a one-third increase in cement prices if pricing aligns with marginal cost. As free allowances are removed, carbon is set to become the dominant cost driver, approaching 40% of opex as free allowances disappear. Based on our plant-level carbon cost curve analysis, which highlights a steep upper tail underscoring an attractive market structure, we think the market will need to rethink where margins could move for large-cap cement. Heidelberg and Holcim (which account for a combined ~40% EU market share) sit at the 30th and 50th percentiles, respectively. Vicat visually looks weaker at the upper end of the cost curve on average (above the 70th percentile). This led to a decline in our 4Q residential investment and government spending tracking. In the Oct durable goods print, core capital goods orders and shipments surprised slightly to the upside. In the Oct and Nov IP report, business equipment and mining came in lower than expected. This led to a decline in our 4Q structures and equipment investment tracking. Also, manufacturing inventories came in lower than expected. records.text: 9 January 2026 UK Weekly Digest Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 role in shaping market expectations. First, fiscal policy. With the Chancellor moving to one single fiscal event in 2026, questions will remain around the credibility of departmental budgets. More fiscal slippage, we think, is likely (marginal) - given our growth and labour market expectations. And we expect some further clean up of the public finances in the autumn. Second, productivity. With public sector capex surging ahead and business investment also on the rise, we will be watching for any tentative signs that productivity growth (TFP) is pushing up again as the economy reaps the benefits of capital deepening. To be sure, with the jobless rate on the rise, and growth holding up relatively well, it may be that we are finally seeing some greenshoots in productivity growth after a stalled decade. Finally, deregulation and market reform. Behind the scenes, the Government alongside the BoE are pushing together a package of broad reforms from its most recent T-Bill consultation to support the gilt market, to potentially lowering leverage ratio requirements for lenders, or through cutting red tape for businesses. Keep an eye on planning reform - which will focus on turning already announced changes into a more permissive, higher capacity system. records.text: M Global Idea Morgan Stanley Research 1 Morgan Stanley Research: Key Forecasts Next 12-Months Outlook: Our High-Conviction Calls Deciphering Economic Momentum: The momentum in US economic growth data stands in contrast to the slow labor market. The strong spending with weak job growth recalls our two upside risk scenarios from our Year-Ahead Outlook. In the first, stronger aggregate demand overpowers the weak labor market, job growth starts to catch up, leading to higher inflation and then eventually some Fed hikes. But if the solid GDP with weak jobs is a reflection of a nascent productivity boom, we might see strong growth with disinflation. Given the step-down in the unemployment rate in December and still-positive job gains, our US Economics team has pushed off more cuts from the Fed. These debates will likely become more prominent as the process for a new Fed Chair progresses in the first quarter. The Year of Risk Reboot: 2026 is poised to be a strong year for risk assets – the triumvirate of easing fiscal, monetary, and regulatory policy should work together in a pro-cyclical way, meaning markets can shift focus to asset class-specific stories. For stocks, the main themes, in the US especially, will be stronger earnings growth and broadening leadership, while AI financing and a revival of M&A will take center stage in credit markets. Macro concerns still matter, but "micro" will become a larger driver of asset returns in this cyclical recovery, in our view. Constructive

records.text: US Economic Weekly | 09 January 2026 3 Where do we stand on tariff collection? Tariff collection has been trending at around $30bn per month, or 1.2% of GDP on an annualized basis (Exhibit 2). Of this, we estimate that roughly 55-65% (0.7-0.8% of GDP) is due to IEEPA. What happens next if the IEEPA tariffs are struck down? If the IEEPA tariffs are struck down, the administration will likely turn to other statutory authorities to recover at least some of the lost revenue. The first step will likely be to resort to Section 122, which allows for a tariff rate of up to 15% for a period of 150 days, after which it would need to be extended by Congress. The administration will likely use this 150-day period to launch additional Section 232 (national security) and 301 (unfair trade practices). In this scenario, we think the result could be a net loss of around 0.3% of GDP in tariff revenues (~$90bn per year). Moreover, the final tariff structure will likely be much lumpier. Some sectors (predominantly those deemed important for national security) could face substantially higher import tariffs because of the Section 232 and 301 investigations. Others (e.g. consumer) could see a big drop in tariff dues. Reversal of the IEEPA tariffs might also give more bargaining power to the US’ trading partners, potentially upending i) the trade deals that the Trump Administration has struck since “Liberation Day”, and ii) ongoing trade negotiations. In principle, Ukraine has sufficient capacity to meet this demand: as of 2022, cement production capacity was 17.7mt, and damage to these facilities appears limited. Domestic supply will therefore be critical for reconstruction. The largest local producer, CRH (covered by Adam Seiden), controls around 46% of capacity. While CRH stands to benefit from higher cement demand, Ukraine accounts for only 17% of its European footprint and about 2% of group sales. Even if rebuilding doubles domestic utilisation, the impact would likely add just 2% to the top line, making the reconstruction supportive but not transformative for CRH’s equity story. Imports have historically played a minimal role in Ukraine’s cement market (~5% penetration between 2012–21), and we see little reason for this to change post-war on account of logistical challenges and under-utilised domestic capacity. Consequently, we expect only limited upside for Eastern European producers (HEI and BZU) from export opportunities into Ukraine, though there may be some minor impact from improved pricing discipline in surrounding markets. 9 January 2026 74 Barclays | European Materials

records.text: Asia Economic Weekly | 09 January 2026 3 Japan in Focus Takayasu Kudo BofAS Japan takayasu.kudo@bofa.com Tax reforms: Small cuts, priority on growth investments The FY26 tax reform blueprint includes cuts to income and corporate tax, in line with proposals from the Takaichi administration and major opposition parties. However, it omits the consumption tax cuts advocated by all major opposition parties in the 2025 Upper House elections, and drastically scales back the income tax cuts the Democratic Party for the People (DPFP) has been calling for. It also builds in alternative sources of funding such as revisions to the existing tax regime and tax hikes, which will limit the net negative impact on tax revenues to ¥710bn (0.11% of GDP). Regarding income tax cuts, the government plans to raise the income tax deduction— often referred to as the “annual income barrier”—with a focus on middle -income households. However, the scope is narrower than what the DPFP has proposed, limiting the additional tax relief to about ¥650bn. As a result, we expect only a modest boost to consumer spending in 2026, given that a ¥650bn tax cut would increase households’ annual disposable income by just 0.2%. Little effect on consumption, support for capex/R&D On the corporate side, the blueprint introduces a new investment incentive scheme and expands R&D tax credits, echoing measures first implemented under the Abe administration. records.text: Inflation Nears the Target as Tariff Effects Fade Our inflation forecast for 2026 is also more optimistic than consensus and is perhaps our most differentiated view. We expect core PCE inflation to fall to 2.1% year-over-year by December and core CPI to fall to 2.0%. Our forecasts are about 0.3pp below consensus, the FOMC, and market pricing. We are confident that inflation will decline in part because we think there was actually meaningful progress in 2025, especially in the shelter category, that was masked by a moderate one-time boost from tariffs that should fade this year. While progress on core PCE inflation has stalled at 2.8% year-over-year, we estimate that passthrough from tariffs to consumer prices has contributed 0.5pp, primarily in goods categories, which implies that inflation excluding the one-time effect of tariffs has already fallen to 2.3%.
