Answering key questions on China’s growth, policy, trade and inflation: China’s real GDP may have been relatively resilient in 2025, growing by an estimated 5%, but its trajectory this year is shrouded in uncertainty, leading to a divergence in market expectations . On the one hand, the recent Central Economic Work Conference (CEWC) mapped out a piecemeal stimulus package that is unlikely to lift the economy significantly (see China: Policy meeting continues piecemeal easing path, dated 12 December 2025). On the other, 2026 marks the start of the 15th Five-Year Plan, which some market participants think could spark a rebound in growth as the authorities potentially front-load investments . Opinions on inflation are also divided. Some argue that the ongoing anti-inflation campaign will reflate the economy, while others question how effective it will be. In this note we address such concerns by answering the 10 most frequently asked questions on topics such as growth, the Five-Year Plan, the recent investment downturn, consumption policies, the trade outlook, as well as inflation momentum . Correlations between US and RoW stocks also tell us that US exceptionalism is alive and well: Since 2020, US equity markets have become increasingly less correlated with other regions, both DM and EM. The shifts are more like swings – correlations went from +0.8 to -0.25 within the course of just five years. We think that several factors are driving this: the US has led in AI developments and adoption, driving index outperformance; the policy environment in the US post-pandemic has also meant that growth has been stronger than in RoW. Over the longer term, the theme of a multipolar world would likely drive regional equity correlations down further, changing the risk profile of global equities (i.e., volatility of the asset class falls as regions become less correlated). Over the shorter term, it makes us convinced that US equities can march to the tune of its own drum and outperform RoW this year.

records.text: PEN: The BCRP has intensified its dollar-buying activity, effectively curbing the appreciation of the PEN. Official BCRP data shows that the bank purchased about USD6bn through direct spot transactions alongside swap operations in just November and December. This scale of intervention is reminiscent only of the commodity boom witnessed in the early 2010s. If the BCRP continues to lean against the wind, the currency appreciation resulting from the multi- year copper price boom may proceed at a more gradual and controlled pace. Additionally, the market is entering the typical election trade window, during which the PEN historically underperforms (the first round is due April 12). EEMEA NBP to stay on hold PLN: We expect the NBP to remain on hold, in line with Bloomberg consensus, and do not anticipate any material change in NBP communication. The governor is likely to highlight the NBP’s data dependence and is unlikely to offer guidance. However, the market still discounts more than two 25bp cuts this year, which seems excessive, in our view. Therefore, we believe that the NBP’s easing pause should put pressure on front-end rates and support the zloty. Consequently, we continue to see value in staying long PLNCZK spot and in paying PLN 2y1y rates versus the Czech equivalent. Our recommendation to pay PLN FRA 6x9 matured with WIBOR 3M at 3.95%; hence, we close our recommendation, marking a theoretical loss of 17bp. Global Economic Weekly | 09 January 2026 17 Emerging EMEA Jean-Michel Saliba MLI (UK) Mai Doan MLI (UK) Vladimir Osakovskiy >> Merrill Lynch (DIFC) Tatonga Rusike MLI (UK) Holiday review Complete report: Emerging Insight: EEMEA – Holiday review 05 January 2026 Poland: scope for slightly more NBP easing amid better disinflation progress We revised our National Bank of Poland (NBP) outlook to include one more 25bp rate cut in spring 2026 to 3.75%, following stronger disinflation trends in recent months. The CPI backdrop is providing more comfort to the NBP, with the December headline inflation easing to 2.4% yoy, below the central bank’s target. The improved near-term inflation optics likely supports the case for a cautious continuation of easing, particularly as inflation expectations remain broadly anchored. That said, the scope for further easing appears constrained by strong domestic fundamentals. Core inflation remains sticky at 2.8% yoy, and wage growth is still hovering around 6-7%. Meanwhile, economic momentum is strengthening, with GDP growth in 4Q tracking close to 4%, and the output gap turning positive. These dynamics point to growing demand-side pressures in the coming year. Together with 175bp total NBP easing in 2025, there is not much more room for further disinflation to justify much deeper rate cuts, in our view. There is some downside risk to our rate call, though we continue to think the floor for the NBP base rate is 3.50%. See our report, CEE Watch: Mixed

records.text: Summary of anti-involution measures in key sectorsQ10: Will the anti-involution campaign have more impact on ending China’s deflation in 2026? We maintain our view that the anti-involution campaign will alleviate, but is unlikely to eliminate, China’s deflationary pressure . The authorities have maintained a soft, market-oriented approach so far in this round of the anti-involution campaign, featuring moral suasion and tighter approval for new capex, without administrative orders for production reduction or shutdowns of over-capacity. As such, supply side pressure has not gone away. Figure 25 summarizes the industry-specific action plans to counter involution. For the steel sector, the government still requires 4% value-added growth and 5% growth for non- ferrous metals in 2025–26, rather than a reduction in output. At the same time, domestic demand, represented by retail sales and fixed asset investment, has further weakened notably after the launch of the anti-involution campaign last July. As a result, the rebalancing of demand-supply has not made much progress and the deflationary pressure in the industrial sector has only been alleviated slightly. Two representative industries in this round of the anti- involution campaign process are solar and auto. Upstream silicon material prices rebounded markedly in July but have largely flatlined since then. records.text: ey Takeaways Incoming activity data point to greater momentum than we assumed. We revise higher our outlook for growth to 2.4% in 2026, from 1.8% previously. The unemployment rate fell in December to 4.4% and November was revised lower to 4.5%. Labor demand remains soft, but slack creation is muted. records.text: Solid GDP Growth as the Tariff Drag Gives Way to a Boost from Tax Cuts We forecast GDP growth of 2.5% (vs. 2.1% consensus) in 2026 on a Q4/Q4 basis or 2.8% (vs. 2.1% consensus) on a full-year basis. We have lowered our 12-month recession probability from 30% to 20%—slightly above the historical unconditional average of 15%—in response to early signs of labor market stabilization, discussed below, and our expectation that the largest policy risks are behind us. The key driver of our forecast for solid growth this year is that the drag from tariff increases should give way to a boost from business and personal tax cuts included in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). Because the fiscal boost will be frontloaded and the end of the government shutdown will provide a mechanical boost of about 1.3pp in Q1, we expect GDP growth to be stronger in the first half of the year. Our forecast assumes that with the midterm elections approaching and the cost of living emerging as a major political theme, the White House will avoid significant further tariff increases. In fact, we expect the effective tariff rate to fall by about 2pp—resulting in a 9.5pp net increase since the start of 2025—because new deals and exemptions could lower the effective tariff rate, and any new tariffs that replace tariffs the Supreme Court might overturn would likely be capped at 15%, below some current rates. records.text: How Technology Creates New Occupations If the results above are a guide to future structural change, it means that even a large AI-related displacement of workers can be absorbed elsewhere if given enough time, particularly via the creation of new work opportunities and occupations. While it is hard to say exactly where “new AI occupations” will emerge, history provides guidance on how technology creates new occupations. First, technology creates new occupations that are directly made possible by technological progress. Exhibit 7 illustrates this dynamic over the last 30-40 years. The left chart shows that more than 6mn workers (almost 4% of total employment) are employed in computer-related occupations—including 2mn as software engineers, 700k as support specialists, 644k as IT systems managers, 599k as IT systems analysts, and 319k as computer programmers—that did not exist in the pre-computer era. The right chart considers new industries that have emerged due to digital technology and the internet but that are less directly tied to computers. records.text: ntil the CPI shelter decelerates to a pace in line with these benchmarks, as rents reset toward market conditions. • We think the logic that CPI rents will slow to a pace resembling these measures is deeply flawed on two grounds. ° Level versus growth rate: This logic is seemingly based on the expectation that the growth rate of CPI rents will eventually converge toward market measures, entirely overlooking the discrepancy in level terms. We show that market rent measures surged more than the CPI measure during the pandemic, opening up a large, positive gap that has been closing only gradually amid slow increases in market measures. Similarly, evidence that market rent measures continue to track above pre-pandemic trend levels also argues against rapid disinflation in CPI rents (Figure 15). ° New leases versus renewals: More importantly, the logic is based on an apples-to-oranges comparison, as market measures primarily capture new leases, which account for only a small share (~10%) of the rental market. Instead, the CPI sample, which is meant to be representative of the entire housing stock, is largely informed by dynamics of renewal leases, which tend to be stickier, and are currently running higher than new-lease rent inflation (Figure 13, Figure 14). Carry considerations amid compressed risk premia. Our economists’ 2026 n baseline for solid growth and disinflation is one that argues for the tails of the distribution remaining in check. Meanwhile, the Treasury supply backdrop appears fairly digestible with the Fed poised to absorb a meaningful portion of the increase in T-bill issuance. With the shift in Fed balance sheet policy also laying the groundwork for a more stable funding environment, the mix of ingredients screens favorably for carry strategies. But there are risks around that benign fundamental path, and the margin for error in certain pockets appears narrow. The key here is the “Domar condition. ” This states that as long as the nominal GDP growth rate exceeds the nominal effective interest rate (interest payments divided by the previous year’s JGB balance), the debt/GDP ratio can be maintained even if the PB is somewhat in deficit. Conversely, if the effective interest rate exceeds the GDP growth rate, a PB surplus is needed to maintain the debt/GDP ratio. Thus, relying on this logic, assuming recent circumstances remain largely unchanged, a certain PB deficit can be justified for FY26, which is convenient for the Takaichi administration in its bid to generate a “high-pressure economy” through fiscal spending. Under the scenario set during the Ishiba administration, the nominal GDP growth rate was projected to exceed the nominal effective interest rate by more than 1pp, making it easy to satisfy the Domar condition ( Figure 21). Since then, under the Takaichi administration, 10y JGB yields have risen further, but there is a considerable lag before higher 10y yields are reflected in the effective interest rate. Therefore, the Domar condition is still expected to be met in FY26. However, how the market perceives fiscal expansion remains a risk. If the government continues to generate fiscal headlines, sustaining upward pressure on long-term yields, the consequences could materialize in later years. Conventionally, Fed chairs step down from their governor position when their term as Fed chair expires. As we had pointed out in prior research, there is a precedent for a former chair to remain as a governor after being replaced by the president. Chair Mariner Eccles resigned as Fed chair in 1948 but continued to serve as governor for another three years. Powell has not yet announced whether he would step down in May. If he stays, it could frustrate the administration’s efforts to reshape the Federal Reserve Board. In our view, Powell’s decision to push back so strongly against what he views as a threat by the administration to the Fed’s independence significantly raises the probability that Powell may remain at the Fed as a governor after the end of his term as chair. We view his statement that “Public service sometimes requires standing firm in the face of threats. No, we expect growth to ease further. From a secular perspective, since 2012 China’s economy has slowed from an average annual expansion of roughly 10% to about 5% in recent years. This structural deceleration is typical of a maturing economy and mirrors the paths taken by Japan, South Korea and Taiwan (see Figure 1). From a cyclical perspective, the economy faces two major sources of headwinds in 2026. After four years’ sharp contraction, even though property sales volumes are now close to their mid-term demand trend, a pronounced cyclical demand-supply imbalance persists (see China’s property downturn: Not following Japan’s path, dated 15 October 2025). Consumer demand for home purchases is at a record low and inventories remain high in both primary and secondary markets . Although the sector’s contribution to GDP is shrinking, it will continue to act as a drag on growth while the market searches for a cyclical bottom. See Q6 for details . The other headwind comes from the unfolding of a capex down-cycle. Industrial capacity utilization has lingered at multi-year lows and manufacturers’ profit margins are the weakest since 2003 (see Figures 2 and 3). records.text: How Concerned Should We Be About a Job Apocalypse? We have extensively argued that generative artificial intelligence (AI) will provide significant boosts to labor productivity and economic growth, primarily from its ability to automate a large share of work tasks. Our baseline estimate—which uses the Department of Labor’s O*NET database to estimate the share of work tasks that can potentially be automated following the full adoption of generative AI—is that AI can potentially replace 25% of all work hours in the economy (over and above normal structural change), with higher exposure among administrative, legal, and computer occupations and lower exposure for manual jobs (Exhibit 1). Our estimates and the broad consensus that AI opens new automation possibilities have raised concerns that AI could lead to widespread and permanent job losses creating a “job apocalypse”. These concerns echo prior predictions from Nobel Prize-winning economist Wassily Leontief that “humans could go the way of horses” due to technological change—a reference to the sharp decline in the horse population used in production shown in the first half of the 1900s (Exhibit 2)—that have reemerged in the current debate around the labor market impacts of AI. Miran has since doubled down on this view, concluding in a December speech that it is "no longer the case" that PCE shelter inflation needs to catch up with measures for new leases (Figure 3), and that, on this basis, he expects a "faster fall" in shelter inflation. With little doubt, a realization of Miran's outlook would put substantial downward pressure on core inflation. Rent inflation accounts for about 40% of the core CPI basket and 17% of the core PCE basket, so a 2pp deceleration in OER and tenant rents would lower the contribution of these categories to %y/y inflation by about 0.8pp for core CPI, and a little more than 0.3pp for core PCE. Although developments with other core inflation components would still matter, this would certainly go a long way to pushing PCE price inflation back toward the Fed's 2% target. Our baseline sees the situation differently: CPI indices for primary rents and OER slow much more gradually, to readings in the 2.6-2.8% range by end-2026, then to 2.3-2.5% by end-2027. Although this would still push %y/y rates more than a percentage point below pre-pandemic norms, downward pressure on overall core CPI measures would be about half the magnitude argued by Miran. “As the economy emerged from the pandemic, demand for housing outstripped supply, and market rents for new tenants jumped. For the purposes of this outlook, when we refer to US hyperscalers, we are referring to 5 IG companies: AMZN, GOOGL, META, MSFT and ORCL. Last year, four of the five names raised $93bn in the public 'vanilla' IG market. If we add off-balance-sheet deals done through corporate JVs/SPVs, that number is ~ $120bn ( Exhibit 10 ). Though MSFT did not issue debt in 2025, $120bn already represents the highest debt issuance for these companies in history. The last time these companies issued in size was in 2020 and 2021 but only at about $35-40bn annually. As a reminder, of these 5 names, only ORCL is BBB rated while the other 4 are very high quality – AA and above. Outside of these hyperscalers, the other issuers we are following in this AI ecosystem are semiconductor-related names. This includes issuers like AVGO and NVDA. In 2025, they issued about $45bn, which is in line with the peaks of 2020 and 2021. Semiconductor names also saw a sizeable y/y jump in issuance last year, though less pronounced than for hyperscalers ( Exhibit 11 ). Together, hyperscaler and semiconductor issuance was approximately $165bn in 2025.

Further cuts but risks of delay/ fewer cuts We continue to expect two cuts in 2026 in March/June to 3.25% on the back of inflation progress. records.text: US Economics 09 January 2026 Citi Research 2 The last release of CPI data for November suffered from substantial measurement issues related to the government shutdown. December data released next week should have fewer issues, at least in some components, but will still be skewed by the effects of missing data. Measurement issues led November CPI to be on the softer side, but CPI in December should reverse some of this downward bias. We expect a 0.27%MoM increase in December core CPI. Goods prices could be on the stronger side, with some rebound also in core non-shelter services. But importantly, the monthly increase in key shelter components (owners’ equivalent rent and primary rents) should be mostly clean of measurement issues. While inflation data will remain harder than usual to interpret for a few months, a monthly increase in core CPI of 0.27% in December could be on the softer end given expectations for some payback from the downward bias on prices in November. Monthly inflation readings in Q1 should also be relatively free of any measurement issues, and we expect to see more slowing in shelter inflation and less residual Q1 strength in services compared to last year. This should further reduce Fed officials’ perceptions of upside risks to inflation, making the choice to cut rates further toward the midpoint of the neutral range much easier. Summary table on the developments of key factors affecting CPI this year Factors Impact on CPI Our views/Latest trend Foreign exchange _ The CNY appreciated 5% against the USD after April’s low, while CNY NEER gained ~3% since July. If sustained, this could trim CPI inflation by up to 0.2–0.3pp in 2026. Energy prices _ Our commodity team had forecast further declines in oil prices this year. For instance, Brent crude oil was expected to average $65 per barrel in 2026, down ~5% from 2025. Property/Housing rents _ We foresee continued weakness in the property sector with no significant policy stimulus to reverse the downward trend in 2026. Meanwhile, CPI housing inflation turned negative in December for the first time since late 2024, pointing to weakening rental market. If productivity stays strong because of diffusion and adoption of AI against a labor market that has been tight for years, strong growth could come with very different implications. The result is “more growth with less inflation.” GDP growth could beat expectations, and yet with enough ability to produce more output with fewer workers, core inflation might continue to fall to the mid-2% range. Perhaps counterintuitively, in this version of the world, soft hiring is not a sign of weakness, but rather a reflection of efficiency gains. For the Fed, a productivity led upswing would not create the tension of having to decide to reverse course. Right now, it is difficult to disentangle how much of the continued solid growth in the economy is from more demand or more supply. In the December job report, job growth was tepid while the unemployment rate fell 0.2pp. The data will be noisy and policymakers pausing cuts seems natural. But over time under this scenario, the disinflation after tariffs have run their course could be meaningful. The result could be a resumption of the easing cycle to below 3%. This is consistent with the view we outlined in our oil price update earlier this week. The call also focused on the perceived surplus, Venezuela, China and OPEC+. The replay is available via this link. The oil market surplus is exaggerated In the expert's view, the estimated surplus on the oil market is exaggerated for several reasons. He anticipates 2026 oil demand growth remaining robust at ~1.2Mb/d, in line with UBSe. He also thinks that the market does not account for the longer shipping routes related to the logistics disruption post sanctions and therefore does not interpret correctly the level of oil on water. records.text: Deutsche Bank Mark Wall | +44 20 7545 2087 | mark.wall@db.com | European Macro Outlook 17 Economic Uncertainty: Not as high as you think, despite everything In 2025, the perception was high uncertainty, in particular in the trade space. Indeed, trade policy uncertainty has been very high. But measures of economic uncertainty are not as alarming. Turning into 2026, a greater divergence looks to be taking hold. China’s ongoing imbalance between strong production and weak domestic demand has prolonged deflationary pressures, as evident in this week’s PPI and CPI reports. While we look for GDP growth to pick up close to a 6%ar in 1H26 (from an upwardly revised 4.4%), supported by a step up in fiscal support, we expect only a modest recovery in consumer demand and deflationary pressures to persist. Core inflation also remains soft in ASEAN. At the same time, inflation momentum has firmed in Korea, Singapore, and Indonesia amid solid growth (especially in the tech-heavy economies), with food and gold prices adding to the upside. As inflation dynamics diverge, monetary policy is also turning less synchronized. In Singa- pore, we see a materially higher risk of MAS tightening (in April or July) while in Korea we recently took out our final rate cut and see the BoK on a prolonged hold. records.text: ve also decelerated somewhat, as in our conceptual illustration, the spread in rent growth between new and continuing properties remains wider than pre-pandemic norms. For modeling, levels specifications are likely to outperform those using growth rates From Figure 12, we also highlight that, with only one exception, all of the market rent indices showed more pronounced acceleration during the pandemic than the CPI. For example, the Zillow and Apartment List peaked at 16-17% y/y, while CPI rents peaked 8.8% y/y. This means that CPI growth rates undercorrected to these measures during that episode. Given this, it stands to reason that CPI will show less pronounced deceleration as we move forward. Rather than comparing growth rates, we think it is better to assess how the "level" of these market rent indicators compare to CPI. In our view, the abrupt adjustment of new leases during the pandemic induced a level discrepancy between the CPI and market measures, and it is plausible that the sharp deceleration of market rents represents the correction of overshoots that will run their course. Indeed, as Figure 15 shows, levels of most of these measures are either still running above their pre-pandemic trend, or are only gradually converging towards it. Sources: Bloomberg, BNP Paribas End-period USDRMB forecast Q1: Why did the RMB strengthen more than expected at the end of last year? Will this continue? The RMB appreciated faster than the market had expected in the final month of 2025, with USDRMB falling by almost 1,000 pips amid thin liquidity. We believe the move was initially driven by a weaker USD. The DXY index declined 1.1% in December, while USDRMB dropped 1.36%. Exporters, which tend to increase their FX settlement into year end, also contributed to RMB strength (see China FX: Next wave of large exporter FX settlements likely in December, dated 23 October 2025). We believe that USD weakness in early to mid-December increased exporters’ willingness to settle more than usual to prevent FX losses. This reinforced RMB strength, explaining why USDRMB did not rebound along with the DXY in the latter half of the month. A lack of clear defensive action from the People’s Bank of China at year end may have also heightened exporters’ concerns that RMB appreciation could persist, prompting additional settlements. The PBoC has continued to deliver lower fixings, instead of setting a flat fixing or having state banks intervene to curb excessive spot movements. records.text: 12 January 2026 FX Blueprint Page 14 Deutsche Bank AG Theme #6: Hawkish CAD, just a fad – buy USD/CAD, buy EUR/CAD Canada has had a strong run of data, contributing to some pricing for a rate hike later in 2026. But take a closer look and the story quickly crumbles. This is still an economy in transition as previous drivers of growth fade, while new drivers aren’t kicking in just yet. The flows side doesn’t look helpful either. Canadian investors remain resolute in seeking offshore exposure, while foreigners' solid buying of Canada debt may be at risk as yields are more attractive elsewhere. We look for USD/CAD to trade above 1.40 again, and for EUR/CAD to return to 1.64. Don’t believe the hype. Canada has posted the best data surprises in G10 over the past month, highlighted by a big Q3 GDP beat and a chunky 0.5% drop in unemployment. But scratch the surface and it unravels. The GDP beat was a function of a big drop in imports, some lumpy government spending, and robust housing investment. Consumer spending and private business capex actually fell, and exports barely rose. October and November data point to a mild drop in GDP, and business surveys are also downbeat. For example, the long-running Ivey PMI is trending around 50, which has historically correlated to zero growth at best (Figure 31). records.text: US Economics Weekly9 January 2026 ab 5 The details of how Plan B could shape up Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 gives the President the power to impose import surcharges of up to 15% for a maximum of 150 days to address a US balance of payment deficit, and be implemented essentially immediately. The authority has not been tested in the courts, and after 150 days, an extension would require congressional approval. Considering the recent Senate majority voting to repeal the tariffs, extension might be difficult. So this authority could roughly keep the tariff structure in place only until June. The existing section 301 investigation into technology transfers to China could be used to keep tariffs on imports from the region essentially unchanged despite the ruling. For deals with several trading partners, the reciprocal rate that has been imposed is 15% for the EU, Japan, and South Korea, which by coincidence is the maximum tariff allowed under section 122. So, a number of these deals could be quickly replicated with the provision, and the universal 10% tariff that has been applied could become a 15% tariff. Combining these actions, we would estimate that the weighted average tariff would be 12.6%, just a smidge below the current estimate for the weighted average tariff. But what happens after 150 days? Within shelter, the components that carry the largest weights are rents of primary residences -- or tenant's rents -- and owners' equivalent rent (OER). The latter , which is intended to capture implicit costs of owner-occupied properties, is especially important, with its weight accounting for about a third of the core CPI index. The measurement methodology contributes to stickiness CPI rents are measured from the housing survey, which, in each month, samples responses from the occupants of about 8000 separate rental units that are intended to be representative of the overall housing stock. For each sampled unit, the BLS determines the change in effective rents, controlling for changes in quality and for charges that do not reflect housing services. The overall sample is divided into six cohorts that are sampled on a rotating basis every six months: January/July, February/August, March/September, April/October, May/November, and June/ December. In the month that each cohort is actively sampled, the rate of rent inflation is determined using the geometric average monthly rate of increase over the six months between observations, which is weighted across units. After a long and protracted buildup, the Budget was delivered smoothly enough to prompt outperformance in UK bonds and the currency. However, with domestic data weakening in the background and the UK lacking the same growth impetus into 2026 as seen elsewhere in Europe, the risk-reward in the pound has once again become skewed to the downside. We also think believe that medium-term implied volatility in EUR/GBP is currently too low. The macro Our framework for sterling continues to comprise of two components: the monetary policy stance which determines the rates-implied fair value for the pound, and the additional risk premium for fiscal and political uncertainty, which has generally resulted in sterling trading weaker than this fair-value metric for the past six months (Figure 13). Regarding the former, the first half of the year is likely to see two more rates cuts from the BoE, with inflation having surprised to the downside of late and set to converge quite quickly to target and peers. The labour market has also deteriorated. This exercise is particularly relevant for a high-ROIC business like IMCD, where incremental growth expectations exert a disproportionate influence on valuation multiples. To illustrate, the valuation gap between a company growing at +1% and one at +2% is modest; however, the gap between +2% and +3% growth is materially larger. Each additional percentage point of growth drives an accelerating impact on enterprise value. Conceptually, firm value can be expressed as: EV=FCF/(WACC−g). Knowing FCF, EV, and WACC allows us to infer the market-implied growth rate. Applying this framework to IMCD’s 2026E earnings and cash flow suggests the market is pricing in a long-term FCF growth of approximately +1.2%, versus a historical five-year average of +3.4%. FY26 initial budget: Spending growth in line with requests The FY26 initial budget proposal also increases general account expenditures, but this mainly reflects higher interest payments due to conservative interest rate assumptions. Further tax revenue growth improves fiscal outlook With Japan's high nominal economic growth likely to boost tax revenue, as of the initial budget the government also forecasts a primary balance surplus for the first time in 28 years. These models yield similar forecasts for CPI rents, provided that we make analogous assumptions about the future trajectory of market rents. For instance, Figure 37 shows the simulated trajectory of rent growth from our unrestricted specification for a scenario where both REIS and ZORI increase at about 0.5% q/q saar through 2017, as in our earlier base case. In this case, OER gradually decelerates to readings in the range of 0.46-0.54 %q/q (0.15-0.18 %m/m) by end-2027 (Figure 38) using both indicators, where the projections using REIS are at the higher end of the range. Our main takeaway from this exercise is that the choice of rent indicator does not pose downside risks to our model-based forecasts, per se. Although one might run simulations where the REIS indicator increases at a slower rate than our scenarios for ZORI, this risk would be better reflected if we ran scenarios involving a slower pace of increase in ZORI, absent a convincing story about why the two indicators would further diverge. 12 January 2026 26 Barclays | US Economics

That is a contrast to the recently released PMI counterpart, which signaled moderating activity into the end of the year. The ISM improvement was wide- spread across the business activity, new orders, and employ- ment indexes, and is indicative of steady growth in the sector following muted readings since the second quarter. A bull case for copper at $7/lb in 2026 hinges on a tight physical market—driven by persistent or worsening supply disruptions—intersecting with stronger-than-expected demand from the energy transition and global growth, all against a backdrop of supportive macroeconomic policy and investor inflows. Elevated supply disruptions: YTD mine supply disruptions are annualising at ~7% relative to the original production target set at the start of this year. Consequently, we forecast mine supply to decline by 1.4% in 2025 before recovering in 2026, supported by mine ramp-ups, restarts and higher grades in the DRC, Mongolia, China and Panama. Our base case assumes mine supply growth of 2.1% in 2026, incorporating a 5% disruption allowance. However, if disruptions remain elevated at 7% (vs 5%), our supply-demand deficit forecast for 2026 would widen to over 1mt. records.text: : stabilizing around full employment • The labor market has been buffeted by shocks to supply (immigration restrictions) and demand (tariff uncertainty, AI, DOGE). In our view, the supply shock is likely to be the bigger driver of soft job growth this year, especially as labor demand starts to recover on the back of fading tariff uncertainty, a positive fiscal policy impulse and consumer resilience. Hence, we have payrolls averaging 30k in 2H25 (partly due to end of DOGE buyout program) and 50k in 2026. Immigration tightening likely lowers breakeven job growth to about 20k, keeping payrolls close to full employment. Hence, we see the u-rate ticking up to just 4.5% in 4Q25, where it should remain in 1H26 before dropping to 4.3% by 4Q26. Fed: two cuts in 2026 but on hold under Powell • The Fed cut rates by 25bp to 3.5-3.75% at its December meeting, as expected. The Fed also announced reserve management purchases of $40bn per month, starting December 12. We think the majority of the committee wants to go back on hold. But Powell’s decision will come down to the downside risks in the spot labor data (unemployment rate). Our base case remains that the Fed won't cut again under Powell. We expect only two more 25bp cuts this year in June and July. This leaves our projection of the terminal rate unchanged at 3.0-3.25%.

Among the big four issuers, France, Italy and Spain all saw a consistent decline in the WAM of issuance, while for Germany, this increased marginally to 9.7y (see Figure 9). Regarding sector splits, there was a clear preference for sovereigns on the 10y, with the share rising to 29% (see Figure 10). Alongside the 10y, the 5y, 7y and 15y sectors saw an increase in the share of issuance. This was offset by a decline in the 2y-3y segment, and the 20y+ segments. In 2026 we think the WAM of issuance in the eurozone may decline further, although gradually. This is based on our view that Treasuries are likely to make an active effort to reduce long-end issuance given the high level of yields, the steepness of long-end curves, and diminishing demand for long-end bonds from the Dutch Pension Fund sector. In line with this view, we estimate the WAM of German issuance to decline in our projections, from 9.7y to around 9.5y in 2026. From other Treasuries, Netherlands has indicated its intention to reduce the WAM of its debt portfolio – the Treasury has lowered its minimum average maturity target from 8y to 7.5y. Weak domestic demand is just one factor behind imports stagnating, in our view. In 2025, nominal imports were down 5.6% relative to their peak in 2022, driven almost entirely by the -10.7% decline in import prices, particularly commodity prices (Figure 19). For example, import prices of oil, gas and iron ore fell by 28.1%, 30.7% and 16% respectively during this period. Import volumes increased by 2.4% in 2023–25, but the growth rate has slowed markedly versus 13.7% in 2019–21,reflecting two forces at play. One is weaker domestic demand. The property sector used to be the biggest consumer of commodities. Its unpresented slump in the past few years has caused a marked decline in commodity demand . Another driving force is domestic substitution, due in large part to the big increase in competitiveness of domestic products. The automobile industry is a prime example. The market share of foreign brands in China has fallen from about 55% in 2021 to about 30% in 2025, due to the rapid ascent of domestic automakers. Glencore would fit the bill most clearly in our view. It has world-class copper assets in Latam in particular, which come with a growth pipeline that could conceivably see production doubling on a 10-year horizon at relatively attractive capital intensities relative to global benchmarks (details here). Rio and Glencore have had abortive merger discussions at various stages historically, most recently in Q4-24 (details here) - as we note above, the change in CEO at RIO potentially removes one sticking point to a deal proceeding. Glencore management would be a willing seller in our view – as CEO Gary Nagle has said, “everything is for sale at the right price” . Its recent copper- focused CMD was an advertisement of the benefits of owning Glencore to both institutional investors and other companies, in our view (details here). records.text: The Fed: A Compromise on Two More Cuts to 3-3.25% If the labor market stabilizes as we expect, the FOMC will likely shift from risk management mode to normalization mode. The large gap between the official inflation rate and the rate exclusive of tariff effects might continue to drive disagreement on the Committee for a while but will eventually close. At that point, the key question would be what the appropriate terminal rate is. The December dot plot showed that FOMC participants had six different opinions. Some will likely see the current policy rate as a reasonable stopping point, while others—possibly including the new chair—might see another 100bp to go. We expect them to meet in the middle, delivering two more 25bp cuts in June and September (vs. our previous forecast of March and June) to 3-3.25%. But we see the risks as tilted to the downside over the next couple of years. We see a low probability of hikes from a starting point where the funds rate is above the median FOMC participant’s estimate of neutral and the labor market is meaningfully softer than late last cycle. But we see a few potential paths to cuts—a majority might eventually conclude that the neutral or appropriate terminal rate is a bit lower than we are forecasting, especially if inflation falls below 2%; a new risk could prompt another series of insurance cuts, of which there have now been three in seven years; or a recession could lead to deeper cuts. Owning foreign assets brings global opportunity, but also currency risk if not fully hedged. The academic and practitioner literature on the topic is plentiful, but few industry standards have emerged. Approaches still vary depending on factors including investor sophistication, risk appetite and portfolio construction philosophy. The first objective for investors is generally to minimize risk, i.e. limit any excess volatility to the target asset arising from undesired currency movements. This explains the popularity of minimum variance optimizations in driving FX hedging decisions. This methodology often suggests that investors should only consider moving into foreign fixed income on a fully hedged basis, given the relative volatility of FX and fixed income securities. The empiric evidence is less clear-cut for equity investors, with the equity/FX correlation driving dispersion in optimal behaviors across pairs and equity indices. This is why we focus on proposing an FX hedging framework for equity investors. records.text: Japan Viewpoint | 09 January 2026 3 Lifting income tax deduction: Minor increase, limited scope The ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and DPFP have reached an agreement on raising the income tax deduction (the "annual income barrier"), a subject of much debate since 2024. The first step will be an increase in the deduction mainly for low-income households in FY25, with a further increase in FY26 mainly targeting middle-income households with annual incomes of around ¥6mn. This will raise the annual income barrier from ¥1.03mn in FY24 to the ¥1.78mn proposed by the DPFP in FY26 (Exhibit 2). However, this is more targeted in scope than the universal increase for all households irrespective of income that the DPFP was calling for, and the additional reduction in FY26 tax revenue therefore will be limited to ¥650bn (¥1.85tn, on top of the ¥1.2tn cut in FY25). This is far smaller than the ¥7.6tn cut that would have resulted from a universal increase (Exhibit 3). We expect a limited boost to consumer spending in 2026 given that a ¥650bn tax cut will boost households' annual disposable income by just 0.2%. However, the increase in the annual income barrier could help alleviate households' tendency to curb working hours to avoid paying tax. records.text: Germany—2026 Outlook: Fiscal Boost Delivers Cyclical Upswing, Structural Headwinds Persist The German economy has broadly stagnated since 2018, and we expect growth of just 0.3% in 2025 (Exhibit 1, left). Next year, however, we expect Germany to grow at 1.1%, meaningfully above our estimate of potential growth and slightly above consensus. We expect fiscal policy to drive an improvement in domestic demand through the year (Exhibit 1, right). While we estimate that the growth drag from US tariffs will have mostly passed by the end of 2025, continued drag from competition with China will likely weigh on net exports. Fiscal Policy Turns Expansionary and Drives Growth About half of next year’s growth stems from expansionary fiscal policy. The German parliament amended the debt brake rules in March 2025 to allow for higher defence and infrastructure investment. This substantially increased the fiscal space available to the new government that entered office in May. We expect the fiscal deficit to widen to 3.7% in 2026 and 3.9% in 2027 after reaching 2.9% in 2025 (Exhibit 2, left). For Germany, these would be the highest deficits outside of recessions in decades. We see only limited risks for the fiscal rollout, as—compared with initial announcements—the fiscal expansion is more focused on subsidies, social spending and tax reductions than on public investment. records.text: 4 Asia Economic Weekly | 09 January 2026 Further tax revenue growth improves fiscal outlook On the revenue side, the government projects FY26 tax revenue of ¥83.7tn, up ¥5.9tn from the initial FY25 budget of ¥77.8tn, driven by strong nominal GDP growth. Sticky inflation, robust wage growth, and solid corporate earnings are expected to drive further increases in consumption, income, and corporate tax revenues. Unless a severe economic downturn occurs, there is also potential for additional upward revisions. The projected increase in tax revenue translates into planned new JGB issuance of ¥29.6tn, up slightly versus the initial FY25 budget but down from the ¥40.3tn in the FY25 supplementary budget. The initial budget therefore forecasts a primary balance surplus for the first time in 28 years; we think this indicates that the government has taken on board concerns about fiscal discipline. We would note that the scope and period for the government’s primary balance forecast differ from the IMF's standards, which are generally used for international comparisons. We would also note that this is only a projection as of the initial budget, and the actual figure will likely worsen as the government spends the FY25 supplementary budget. However, we think Japan's 2026 fiscal deficit even based on IMF standards will remain lower than other major developed economies that are pursuing procyclical fiscal policies. records.text: 12 January 2026 FX Blueprint Page 4 Deutsche Bank AG Theme#1: Continental Drift – neutral EUR/USD We start the year tactically neutral on EUR/USD, as bullish versus bearish risks are evenly balanced for now. Positive global growth consistent with weaker USD. Last year saw global growth convergence driven by downgrades to US expectations (immigration slowdown, tariffs) but more importantly upgrades to the rest of the world, especially Europe. It is unlikely growth differentials narrow further this year, but our outlook is consistent with resilient global growth, historically associated with a weaker USD (Figure 1). Importantly, the loss of the dollar's high-yielding status should mean that the tailwind of the world's highest DM carry is no longer supportive of the USD. More upside to $ hedge ratios. There was a large increase in European hedge ratios on US assets in 2025. It is unlikely the magnitude of this is repeated, but hedge ratios should continue to rise. The correlation between the USD and the underlying asset that is owned is the key driver of medium-term hedging decisions. A series of negative global shocks has kept the $-equity correlation unusually negative over the last ten years (Eurozone crisis, COVID, Russia invasion of Ukraine), but historically this correlation has been closer to zero. Overall, the December PMI data does not change the key narratives for the euro area economy. The bifurcation between a robust domestic economy, supported by a strong labour market, and a manufacturing sector facing headwinds from a strong currency and tariff adjustments, remains firmly in place. This is consistent with the European Central Bank's latest projections. While cost pressures are picking up, particularly in services where wage growth was noted as a driver in Germany, these are not being fully passed on to consumers, suggesting a squeeze on corporate profit margins. The data reinforces the view that domestic demand should continue to support the economy through 2026, offsetting the persistent weakness in the external-facing sectors. This week's German factory orders provided a significant upside surprise, rising 5.6% MoM (BBG cons: -1.0%). The increase was driven by a strong 7.9% jump in capital goods orders, which have now climbed 13% over the past two months. Even when stripping out volatile components like motor vehicles, air, and space, the underlying trend remains robust, suggesting a notable pickup in industrial activity. The primary driver behind this surge appears to be government defence procurement. records.text: EM – LOC AL EY ES F OR A GLOBAL VI EW 709/01/2026 Q6: Has the rise in China’s high-tech sector offset fully the slump in the property sector? No, we think China’s rising high-tech sector still does not compensate fully for the drag on growth caused by the housing market slump. Here we only analyze the impact of the decline in property development on economic growth — we don’t consider other activities related to housing supply such as leasing and management. Since property development has a long supply chain, we assume investment itself has a 1.5x multiplier. After four years of huge contraction, the share of the property sector has fallen from about 18% of GDP to 9% in 2025. The 16% decrease in property investment translates to a 1.8pp subtraction of GDP in 2025. On the flip side, the share of high-tech sectors has been rising steadily. We use the output of “patent-intensive” sectors defined by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), which includes seven sectors (e.g. IT services, IT equipment, high-end equipment manufacturing, pharmaceuticals) as a proxy of high-tech sectors. In 2024, these sectors represented 13.4% of GDP. If we assume they grew by 8% in 2025, their contribution to GDP would be 1.1pp last year. Therefore, although the share of high-tech sectors in GDP has already surpassed that of property development, it has not been able to offset fully the drag from property development, given the latter has experienced a much sharper decline (Figure 16). Not only consumption has outperformed, but also non-residential private investment. This dynamic is mostly driven by AI-related sectors, which in part explains the rally in the US stock market. Notice that a correction in AI-related stocks can trigger a reassessment of the expected investment in AI, further impacting on the economy through the non-residential investment channel. The first test will come next week with the inflation and retail sales prints. We expect inflation to remain persistent. The Cross-Border Equity Flow Indicator (xbEFI) measures the purchases and sales of equities by institutional investors, and is produced on a daily basis with a two day publication lag. The Cross -Border EFI focuses on trades by investors with base currencies that differ from a stock’s settlement currency. The indicator also includes transactions where the investor’s base currency is the same as the currency in which the trade is settled, and the settlement currency is different from that of the stock’s country of incorporation. An example of such a trade would be the purchase of a Dutch company’s American Depositary Receipts by a U.S. dollar-based fund. The Sovereign Bond Flow Indicator (SBFI) measures the purchases and sales of domestic and foreign sovereign bonds by institutional investors across countries and in regional aggregates and is available in unweighted and duration -weighted forms. We use unweighted flows in this document to capture the most relevant variable for a currency view. The SBFI is updated daily with a two-day publication lag. We use cross-border sovereign bond flows where available and total sovereign bond flows for all other countries.

For instance, a eurozone investor allocating to UK equities would have seen Sharpe ratios of 0.44 on an unhedged basis, 0.42 on a fully hedged basis, 0.48 using our baseline MVO and 0.44 using our tilted MVO. The analysis was run from January 2005 to November 2025. The tables highlight the great dispersion of outcomes that can result from FX hedging decisions. To take an extreme example, an Australian investor taking an unhedged position in Japanese equities would have seen a meagre 0.21 Sharpe ratio increase to 0.6 if fully hedged. On average across all permutations, a full hedge performed better than no hedging (Figure 1, page 1). A dynamic hedge would have showed in-between performance, slightly better than no hedging but worse than a full hedge with decent dispersion across investor base currencies and local equity investments. There is clear value in tilting hedging ratios through a multi-factor FX model. We find that this holds across most G10 permutations. records.text: 9 January 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Deutsche Bank AG Page 5 On the political front, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will be visiting Denmark next week to discuss Greenland. No exact date for the trip has been announced yet. French budget. The government officially resumed its 2026 budget negotiations under a special "bridge law." The formal parliamentary debate is set to begin on January 13, with the government aiming for the bill's passage by the end of the month, which will involve 3 votes on the budget bill. The current version of the bill, as adopted by the Senate in December, targets a budget deficit of 5.3% of GDP. There is now some official acknowledgment that the State budget may not secure a normal parliamentary vote. That leaves the government with two options: the use of the constitutional tool known as Article 49.3 (the budget passes if the government survives a no-confidence vote), or publishing decrees (Article 47.3 - the budget passes automatically but most political groups have stated their intention to censure the government in response). While the special law initially provides for a deficit of 5-5.4%, any extension beyond a few weeks would see the deficit rise as temporary 2025 tax measures expire. Given the political dynamics and the cost of securing support, the final 2026 budget deficit is expected to land at or above 5% of GDP, suggesting limited fiscal consolidation for the year (our forecast is 5.3%). records.text: US Economic Presentation12 January 2026 ab 14 Source: USATRADE, Haver, UBS calculations Trade: imports holding up, a big increase in tariffs Imports have been volatile, but the level isn’t all that dented despite a large hike in tariffs. The economy is likely yet to adjust to this tax hike. • Net exports shaved 4.7 pp off Q1 real GDP growth, then added 4.8 pp to Q2 GDP. Q3 real GDP was boosted 1.6pp. It's obscured what is unfolding in the economy. • One thing is clear. The sizeable decoupling of the US from global trade we though might unfold following the April 2 announcements has not transpired. While we expect imports to suffer from the tariffs in the coming few years, the looming adjustment looks pretty modest. • We estimate that the current set of tariff policies in place would imply a weighted-average tariff of 13.2% using 2024 import shares. That 13.2% rate we estimate is up from 2.5% at the turn of the year, and represents a 1.1% of GDP tax on imports. We estimate slippage to be roughly 1 pp, and our projection assumes a 12.2% effective tariff based on 2024 imports. • That baseline assumption for our projections represents a 10.1 pp increase or a roughly 1.1 pp of GDP tax. From that we estimate the 0.8 pp reduction in real GDP growth spread over four years but predominantly in 2025 and 2026. But a crucial—if under- stated—microeconomic push is underway, laying the ground- work for a sustained investment revival after years of stagna- tion. By the third quarter of 2025, fixed investment, though down sequentially on a seasonally adjusted basis, remained nearly 9% above the 2004–2024 average and 2% higher than the lev- els recorded in the fourth quarter of 2023, when President Milei assumed office (Figure 1). The brisk, V-shaped rebound observed since 2Q24 through the first quarter of 2025 was derailed by a series of policy shocks, which weighed on capex. These ranged from the foreign exchange disruptions tied to the IMF program in April to the exceptionally tight monetary conditions that persisted through the third quarter, culminating in the run-up to the midterm elections. records.text: EM – LOC AL EY ES F OR A GLOBAL VI EW Q5: Will the material boost to consumption from fiscal subsidies continue in 2026? No, we expect it to ease in 2026, primarily due to the boost from the consumer goods subsidy program fading. 1) The subsidy’s size appears smaller than last year. The first batch of special CGBs earmarked for the program is RMB62.5bn for Q1. Assuming an even split across the four quarters, the annual quota would total RMB250bn — a 16.7% reduction on last year. The program also cuts home-appliance coverage from 12 categories to 6 and moves car subsidies from fixed amounts to a percentage of the selling price, reducing support for low-priced cars. 2) The fiscal multiplier of the trade-in subsidy is expected to be lower. We expect the multiplier to fade over time, estimating it at about 1.45x for 2025, down from 2.25x in Q4 2024 when the program began. Moreover, eligibility criteria are tighter, excluding level-2 efficiency home appliances. As such, we forecast the fiscal multiplier to fall further to 1.2x in 2026. Factoring in the above, we expect the program to boost private consumption by 0.5pp in 2026, down from a 0.8pp increase in 2025 (Figure 15). The boost from childcare support measures will be stable. The U-6 rate fell from 8.7% to 8.4%, partially reversing the Nov spike but number of people unemployed for 27 weeks+ did go up. Goods sector layoffs & stable but narrowly driven services Admittedly, after the shutdown related distortions, job growth in the cleaner Dec print looks dismal. Education and health (14k) continued to lead the way. In line with our view, leisure & hospitality surged to 47k due to robust holiday spending and air travel. US Economics Apples and oranges in the CPI basket: Why market rent gauges mislead on shelter CPI rents have been gradually slowing for some time now, and pricing anticipates more of the same given market rent indicators. While many stress downside risks, we think the upside is underappreciated, given indications that rents for higher turnover properties overshot others during the pandemic. • Inflation markets are pricing the return of CPI inflation to target-consistent levels over the course of 2026. A big part of the rationale is an expectation that the gradual deceleration of CPI rents over the past few years will continue. These conditions will maintain downward pressure on manufacturing investment. How growth evolves depends to what extent government policies can counteract cyclical and structural forces, we argue. The official statement that an annual 4.17% GDP growth for the 10 years to 2035 will be enough to fulfil the 2035 objectives signals policymakers’ willingness to accept slower growth. Last month’s 2026 Central Economic Work Conference adopted a more conservative tone than its 2025 counterpart, emphasizing fiscal sustainability and the need to preserve policy space for adverse scenarios. Consequently, we forecast net fiscal stimulus falling from 0.9pp of GDP in 2025 to just 0.2pp in 2026. Monetary policy may be slightly more accommodative: we anticipate a 20bp rate cut in 2026 (versus a 10bp cut in 2025). However, overall policy support will be weaker than last year (for more, see China: Policy meeting continues piecemeal easing path, dated 12 December 2025). Given the combined structural slowdown, the two cyclical drags and a more restrained policy stance, we forecast GDP growth slowing to 4.7% in 2026. The turning point (Y0) was 1973 for Japan, 1992 for Taiwan, 1995 for South Korea and 2012 for China. As a result, the bar for additional easing is now higher, particularly given the divided views on whether unemployment or inflation pose the greater risk. Even so, the Fed has gained confidence in the prospect of a soft landing, as perceived risks around growth, labour markets, and inflation all moderated into year‑end (Figure 1). With fewer downside risks, the F ed is increasingly comfortable with the prospects of a soft - landing given the latest Summary of Economic Projections which point to firmer growth, lower unemployment, and further progress on inflation. Figure 1 Gaining more confidence in a soft-landing Source: State Street Markets, Bloomberg, FOMC BACK TO PARALYSIS OR MORE EASING? For now, the market has two cuts priced for 2026, with the first expected no earlier than April and a second anticipated in the fall. This contrasts with the FOMC’s projections, which signal just one cut this year. Over the next few months, however, conviction is high that the Fed will remain on hold. Options markets assign roughly a 60% probability to no change through Q1, with only about a 35% chance that cuts resume sooner (Figure 2) . At the extremes, the lowest‑probability scenario implies a recession with rates falling well below neutral —reinforcing that both the market and the FOMC are broadly aligned in expecting a soft landing. Such a presumption disregards the gap in the relative levels of these indices that opened during the huge runup of market rents in the aftermath of the COVID-19 lockdowns: From late 2020 to mid-2022, the ZORI index posted a cumulative increase of nearly 20%, during which monthly increases exceeded the pace of CPI rents by as much as 1.5pp per month. This discrepancy opened a gap that persists to this day (Figure 21). If we use the normalizing assumption that there was no gap in February 2020, the shortfall between the two CPI rent measures and the ZORI peaked at about 11.7% in June 2022, and through September 2025 had narrowed by about two-thirds, to about 4%. We see a flat services reading, with balanced risks around our estimate. Overall, the flat monthly reading would be consistent with a 0.1%Q contraction in 4Q. We do pencil in some growth in December, but we note that retailers, on average, reported flat volumes over Christmas trading, with sales up due to inflation. Next week's BRC survey should provide more clues around year-end retail sales. High-frequency tracking suggests a brighter end to the year in the leisure sector, and we do note that those companies will be reporting their year-end results next week. RICS house balance, we think, might drop a touch, given evidence from Nationwide and Halifax on a challenging year-end for the housing market. Elsewhere, Deputy Governor Ramsden and external MPC member Taylor are scheduled to speak next week. Ramsden is speaking on the "proportional resolution regime", and we are uncertain whether he will comment on monetary policy. We think Taylor, however, will, with the title of his speech suggesting commentary on inflation and the labour market. First, our 4Q US GDP tracking estimate now stands at 2.2%, bringing growth in 2025 to 2.4% 4Q/4Q. This is not much different than the 2.5% observed in 2024. That said, and as we noted above, the distortions from volatile trade and inventory flows on the back of tariffs likely clouds the picture. Final sales to domestic purchasers, which is measured as GDP less trade and inventories and is a clearer representation of domestic output, slowed from 3.0% in 2024 (4Q/4Q) to 1.8% in 2025. Second, we pass through some of the strength in consumer spending to our outlook for the US economy in 2026 and 2027. We now forecast growth in real GDP of 2.4% this year and 2.1% next year (both 4Q/4Q, up from 1.8% and 2.0%, previously). Our revised forecast has final sales to domestic purchasers accelerating from 1.8% in 2025 to 2.2% in both 2026 and 2027.

The spread signal is calculated as the ratio of the current spread relative to the prior one-year median spread. The values are then smoothed using a 20-day moving average. For example, a multiple of 1 indicates that the current average spread is equal to the historical median spread for that currency pair, whereas a multiple reading of 2 indicates that the current average spread for that given currency pair is twice as wide as its historical median. Turbulence is a price-based measure of the joint unusualness of G10 currency returns. It captures spikes in volatility in individual market components as well as correlation breakdowns – atypical co-movements – between these components. FY26 initial budget: Spending growth in line with requests The government's initial FY26 budget draft includes a ¥7.1tn (6.2%) increase in total general account expenditure to ¥122.3tn, from ¥115.2tn in the initial FY25 budget, but it is slightly below the ¥122.3tn total of ministries' budget requests submitted in August 2025. The increase in the budget largely reflects higher government debt servicing costs and local government tax grants, rather than a rise in general expenditures. In terms of Oil price impact - our Global team suggests near-term impact likely limited but medium-term risk skews bearish. In the short term, political upheaval often causes some production losses. From its November peak, production has already declined by ~0.2 mb/d and there may be some further downside in the short term. However, the global oil market is likely 2-3 mb/d oversupplied in 1H26 already, so that can probably be absorbed without too much price impact. However, over the medium term, risks to production are clearly to the upside, at least from a resource and technical perspective. The team's current forecast is for Brent to fall to the mid-US$50s in the coming months. Upside to Venezuela's production would add to that cautious outlook. For Treasury Bills (TBs), the MoF has reduced the total issuance of 6- and 12-month TBs from JPY49.2tn in the supplementary budget to JPY40.8tn. Notably, while 12-month T-bills were previously all TBs, the MoF will begin issuing 12-month Financing Bills (FBs), allowing for more flexible adjustment of T-bill maturities. As part of the latest CBAM update, the EC has set out plans to expand the scope of CBAM to downstream products from 2028 (there will be a two-year pilot process, similar to CBAM for direct imports, so that importers can get used to administrative requirements). The bulk of these downstream products are within the industrial supply chain, with a small share for household goods (e.g. washing machines). There is also a potential adjustment to policy whereby EU installations exporting goods to other countries will receive a reimbursement for a portion of carbon costs to prevent exports being crowded out by third-party products that don't include any carbon cost. Details remain very thin on how much reimbursement will be possible, but this in theory helps limit the risk of carbon leakage. With that said, we think much of the decline in European manufacturing competitiveness is driven by energy costs, and to an extent a lack of innovation, which carbon reimbursement might not solve. We think the wide ASW in POLGBs, particularly around 10y, is justified given the increase in domestic fixed rate issuance in recent years (Figure 7). Issuance above 5y particularly increased over the past year and the 2027 elections likely limit the room for a reduction in issuance. Carry on POLGB ASW increases: The carry on the 4y ASW has improved and now sits at multi-year highs, helped by a dovish NBP which has delivered 100bp of easing since September. Carry on the 4y ASW has improved both from a local (funding at 3m Wibor) and foreign (funding at 3m FX I/Y) perspective (Figure 8). Carry, from a local perspective, matters because local banks remain the largest holders of Polish government securities, owning around 50% of the total outstanding. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 09 January 2026 15 Japan Takayasu Kudo BofAS Japan Complete report: Asia Economic Weekly: Japan’s budget: Temporary relief from fiscal concerns 09 January 2026 Tax reforms: Small cuts, priority on growth investments The FY26 tax reform blueprint includes cuts to income and corporate tax, in line with proposals from the Takaichi administration and major opposition parties. However, it omits the consumption tax cuts advocated by all major opposition parties in the 2025 Upper House elections, and drastically scales back the income tax cuts the Democratic Party for the People (DPFP) has been calling for. It also builds in alternative sources of funding such as revisions to the existing tax regime and tax hikes, which will limit the net negative impact on tax revenues to ¥710bn (0.11% of GDP). Regarding income tax cuts, the government plans to raise the income tax deduction— often referred to as the “annual income barrier”—with a fo cus on middle-income households. However, the scope is narrower than what the DPFP has proposed, limiting the additional tax relief to about ¥650bn. As a result, we expect only a modest boost to consumer spending in 2026, given that a ¥650bn tax cut would increase households’ annual disposable income by just 0.2%. records.text: Another risk is that companies are increasingly discussing layoffs and appear eager to use artificial intelligence (AI) to reduce labor costs. Because AI does not seem to have been a major driver of the decline in job growth so far, an increased reluctance to hire in anticipation of AI being able to replace workers in the near future would represent a new obstacle to maintaining full employment. As a result, we see a period of jobless growth similar to the “jobless recovery” of the early 2000s as a plausible alternative to our baseline scenario. What might this look like? In the past, faster technological progress has tended to lead to somewhat greater occupational turnover and consequently somewhat higher frictional unemployment. But the pick-up in productivity growth resulting from faster technological change has also tended to put additional temporary downward pressure on inflation, allowing the Fed to keep the funds rate a bit lower to support the labor market through these transitions. There is no guarantee that AI will follow this average historical pattern—it could displace jobs too quickly for policymakers to respond effectively or it could create a more difficult trade-off between full employment and low inflation—but past experience is at least mildly reassuring. records.text: 12 January 2026 FX Blueprint Page 18 Deutsche Bank AG Theme#8: All star lineup – buy TRY, ZAR, CZK, ILS, EGP, UZS Our DB EM FX total return index was up 16% last year. This was - by 3% - the best performance since we have had data to track EM returns from 2000. By far we believe the strongest reason to be cautious on emerging market currencies is therefore the not-quite-iron law of FX mean reversion. But, casting our eye over the relevant drivers of volatility and returns, in our view this is really the only pressing one. Moreover, while recent years have seen variable annual EM FX returns, 2001- 2007 was characterised more often than not by sequential gains (Figure 43). So we stick with our constructive view, although we prefer currencies positively exposed to improving growth. Commodity price moves are bullish for emerging markets. We were very positive at the end of last year about the positive growth outlook for EM, especially in the CEEMEA region, owing to German fiscal stimulus, falling energy prices and easier financial conditions. Unfor- tunately, our experience watching the wage data in Israel sug- gests that (i) relying on one or even a few data points to gauge wage developments may be deceiving, and (ii) there is no good, easy way to smooth through the noise in the wage data. For instance, wage data is available for 107 sectors in which Israeli citizens are employed. This large cross-section should in principle allow one to extract some measure of central ten- dency in wage dynamics, especially if one suspects that growth is affected by heavily-weighted sectors (like high- tech) or changes in weights. However, our estimates of medi- an wage momentum across these sectors points to very small reduction in the volatility relative to the headline average wage growth indicator. Even a brief glance at the average wage series would suggest that there has been little change in the underlying trend. records.text: US Economics Weekly9 January 2026 ab 3 US Economics Weekly UBS Research Economic Comment: what's next for tariffs? Despite speculation building that the Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) would issue an opinion this morning on the legality of tariffs imposed by the administration under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), they did not. Should the tariffs be ruled illegal, the administration could no longer continue to collect revenues for tariffs enacted via IEEPA, and we estimate this accounts for ~2/3 of new revenues. The tariffs imposed with IEEPA include fentanyl tariffs on imports from China, border tariffs on Canada/Mexico, the universal tariff, reciprocal tariffs, those tariffs in deals and the removal of the de minimis exemption. We estimate the amount of federal revenue that might need to be refunded could be as high as ~$150bn, but any refund process would likely be drawn out, and we expect this would likely be sent back to the lower courts by the SCOTUS. More on that below. We expect a large majority, if not all, of the IEEPA tariffs could be reconstructed using other trade authorities, as has been referenced by many in the administration in recent months (comments from Treasury Secretary Bessent here and USTR Greer here). Put simply, we are not simulating an exogenous shock to all market interest rates, narrowing the channel through which $200bn in purchases of agency mortgage-backed securities can influence economic outcomes. The housing sector, in terms of residential investment, is only about 3.8% of GDP, about half of its peak prior to the global financial crisis. A second reason the effects are small is that the FRB/US model assumes households behave in a gradual manner when adjusting their holdings of durable goods and housing, as do firms when investing in productive capital. Incorporating gradual behavior reduces the amplitude of the response, but also elongates the response. Third, as noted above, we are simulating a transitory shock to the mortgage rate. Households and firms are likely much less sensitive to transitory changes in income and sales. Economic theory suggests households and firms are less willing to respond to changes in interest rates that are viewed as temporary because of habit persistence and adjustment costs.

records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W 212/01/2026 Local banks still top holders: Domestic banking systems in the CE3, especially Poland and the Czech Republic have played an ever-larger role in local government bond markets. Their share of holdings is at or near multi-year highs, also as a share of their asset base (Figure 2). At the margin, they have also been the main absorbers of increased government bond issuance since the pandemic. The absolute level of holdings may be high, but we think it can increase further while loan-to-deposit ratios continue to decline, government bonds continue to receive favourable regulatory treatment and as the carry/roll on bond holdings improves as CE3 curves steepen (see EM: How local bonds carry when funded with FX points, dated 1 August 2025). Foreign participation muted: CE3 local government bonds did not see large foreign inflows in 2025 (Figure 3). The share of outstanding bonds held by nonresidents is at or close to historical lows across the CE3 (Figure 4). The lack of enthusiasm was notable in a year when EM performed very strongly – the GBIE1001 Index rose 19%, with CE3 local government debt also outperforming. In CZGBs, foreign holdings actually decreased y/y as of November 2025, while in Poland the increase in the level of foreign holdings (Figure 3) lagged the increase in total debt outstanding, resulting in a historically low foreign share of total holdings at 12%. In the past seven weeks, the series has seen a period of volatility surrounding the Thanksgiving and now Christmas and New Year's Day holidays, and we may not quite be out of the woods. In our preview (link here) we wrote that we assumed that initial claims would see a similar not-seasonally-adjusted inflow this year as after New Year's Day 2025, but would be met with a notably smaller seasonal factor, leading to a modest seasonally-adjusted increase. That appears to have been roughly realized in this morning's data. The holiday season sees the largest not-seasonally-adjusted changes in filings all year, and the seasonal factors often have difficulty picking up the timing shifts adequately. With this week's data, the 4-week moving average fell 7K to 212K, as the rebound the week ending December 6 fell out of the moving average. We would warn against extracting much signal from claims until the noise abates.

As regulatory reforms and improved market access attract greater foreign direct investment, Argentina stands to benefit from enhanced innovation, knowledge transfer, and integra- tion into global value chains. If these trends persist, and con- struction investment recovers, Argentina could see potential growth rise toward the 4–4.5% range over the medium term, from our current 2.5% estimate. A sustained investment revival—anchored by policy credibility and structural reforms—will be essential to unlocking Argentina’s latent growth potential and reducing macroeconomic vulnerabilities over time. While the outlook for investment and potential growth is increasingly constructive, risks remain. The sustainability of the investment revival will depend on the government’s abili- ty to maintain macroeconomic stability, advance its reform agenda, and secure access to both external and domestic financing. Any reversal in the supportive macro backdrop, renewed policy uncertainty, or external shocks could weigh on capital formation and slow progress toward higher poten- tial growth. As such, ongoing policy credibility and tight fis- cal management will be critical to ensuring that Argentina’s investment momentum translates into durable gains in pro- ductivity and long-term output. records.text: 6, we expect almost all companies to face a choice between cutting the dividend or holding the dividend flat in an environment where some industry forecasts point to further declines in 2026 or risking higher leverage, which is already >2x on average. Headline dividend yields of 5-9% in some names seem to reflect market scepticism rather than strength as companies in the sector which have historically held strong commitments are increasingly at odds with fundamentals. • Despite structural headwinds and elevated long-term dividend risk, we do see a tactical opportunity for investors with a 6- to 12-month horizon. We expect most diversified chemical companies to declare their FY25 dividends in Q1 2026, to be paid in May/June. Once declared, these dividends are highly unlikely to be reversed, even if market conditions do deteriorate in 2026, because doing so would be reputationally damaging and legally complex. This creates a window where investors may be able to lock in headline yields of 7-9% (Evonik, Solvay, Arkema) with relatively high confidence of receiving the payout, if a company chooses to hold their 2025 dividends constant. Ultimately, the risk then lies primarily in share price volatility, not dividend cancellation. For investors willing to accept sector volatility and avoid overextending beyond mid-2026, we believe this dividend capture strategy could deliver attractive cash returns even as the longer-term outlook remains challenging. 9 January 2026 9 Barclays | Euro
