LLC Arunima Sinha Global Economist Arunima.Sinha@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-4125 Mayank Phadke, CFA Economist Mayank.Phadke@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-1531 December Employment: Par for the Course Canadian employment was flat in December. The Canadian economy is confronted by structural challenges including materially weaker population growth, and we expect a range of low employment prints going ahead. We see this December print as first of many modest prints, and continue to expect the BoC to remain on hold in 2026. Key Takeaways • In December, the Canadian economy added 8.2k jobs, all of them in goods-producing sectors. The unemployment rate ticked up, but remains close to the lower end of its recent range- we attribute much of the increase to an increase in the participation rate. • Recent prints continue to affirm that weakness from trade-related sectors is not spilling over to the broader economy. At the same time, we note that these levels of employment growth fall within the standard error of estimates (31.6k), unlike the past three months, and we do not take a strong signal from the headline numbers. • The structural drag from slowing population growth remains ahead of us. Population growth has slowed to 9.9k (1.3%Y)- outside of Dec'20- a series low going back to 1976. 2026 and 2027 will see the population growth slow from over 3% to a standstill, reducing employment gains to as low as 5-15k per month.

For gold, the most important dynamic remains in play – inelastic official demand displacing price-sensitive jewellery demand, elevating prices more quickly than model and dollar-beta would predict. In Q4 IMF data Finland, Brazil and Poland reported gold purchases, with total central bank purchases of 3.3 mm troy oz against 0.3 mm troy oz of sales, Figure 59. This puts the 3m annualised pace above the long-run average, Figure 60, and suggests the World Gold Council's Q4 estimate could be the highest of the year. Clearly, elevated gold prices are not yet detracting from reserve managers' inclination to accumulate gold, consistent with WGC and OMFIF surveys. records.text: 2026 US Economic Outlook: Solid Growth, Low Inflation, Shaky Labor Market The US economy appears to have grown more than 2% in 2025, similar to consensus expectations at the start of last year but a faster pace than looked likely after large tariffs were announced last spring. One reason that the economy beat those early April expectations is that the White House scaled back the largest tariffs that would have been the most economically disruptive. But another is that while the tariffs did act like a tax increase and create uncertainty for businesses, some of the potential negative effects of tariffs that historical experience might have suggested did not amount to much—foreign retaliation was limited, the dollar depreciated instead of appreciating, and the stock market eventually moved past tariff concerns. There is a prominent alternative narrative that the boom in artificial intelligence investment simply offset the tariff blow and powered much of last year’s GDP growth, but its impact was actually quite limited, in part because some of it is missed in the GDP statistics. While the economy performed well from a GDP perspective, 2025 looks different from a labor market perspective. Job growth slowed sharply last year, and the unemployment rate rose somewhat. Our strongest conviction views for 2026 are our above-consensus GDP growth forecast and our below-consensus inflation forecast. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 09 January 2026 5 Where do we stand on tariff collection? Tariff collection has been trending at around $30bn per month, or 1.2% of GDP on an annualized basis (Exhibit 2). Of this, we estimate that roughly 55-65% (0.7-0.8% of GDP) is due to IEEPA. What happens next if the IEEPA tariffs are struck down? If the IEEPA tariffs are struck down, the administration will likely turn to other statutory authorities to recover at least some of the lost revenue. The first step will likely be to resort to Section 122, which allows for a tariff rate of up to 15% for a period of 150 days, after which it would need to be extended by Congress. The administration will likely use this 150-day period to launch additional Section 232 (national security) and 301 (unfair trade practices). In this scenario, we think the result could be a net loss of around 0.3% of GDP in tariff revenues (~$90bn per year). Moreover, the final tariff structure will likely be much lumpier. Some sectors (predominantly those deemed important for national security) could face substantially higher import tariffs because of the Section 232 and 301 investigations. Others (e.g. consumer) could see a big drop in tariff dues. Reversal of the IEEPA tariffs might also give more bargaining power to the US’ trading partners, potentially upending i) the trade deals that the Trump Administration has struck since “Liberation Day”, and ii) ongoing trade negotiations. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W 5 Leveraging a factor model for FX equity hedging We study the risk-adjusted performance of four FX hedging frameworks for equity investors: • Equity investment in local currency, on an unhedged basis. The investor takes on the full FX risk associated with the equity allocation (spot changes). • Equity investment in local currency, fully hedged. The investor is not exposed to changes in FX spot moves, but bears the carry cost of rolling FX forward positions. The carry cost may be positive or negative depending on the FX forward curve. • Equity investment in local currency, with a dynamic hedge computed using a one-year rolling minimum variance optimization with no return expectations. The dynamic hedge is driven by changes in the local equity market / FX covariance. The investor is exposed to spot moves for the allocation’s unhedged portion and to carry and transaction costs for the dynamic FX hedge. This is our baseline MVO. • Equity investment in local currency, with a dynamic ‘tilted’ hedge computed using a one-year rolling minimum variance optimization. We use the allocation of our multi-factor G10 FX model to inform the ‘return’ side of the MVO optimization and a similar one-year rolling estimate of the local equity market / FX covariance. records.text: Copper trade flows into US could exacerbate physical tightness: US copper inventories have risen on strong imports, driven by expectations of future tariff implementation. This has reduced global visible inventories ex-US (SHFE+LME+China bonded) to ~3 days of consumption, down from 4.5 days at the start of the year. Typically, visible copper exchange stocks build seasonally in the first quarter as supply continues while demand slows – particularly during the Northern Hemisphere winter and the Chinese Lunar New Year, when downstream fabricators and manufacturers temporarily curtail activity while smelters maintain operating rates. However, recent mine supply disruptions concentrated in Q4-25 and Q1-26 could prevent the usual seasonal build if smelters receive less feed and refined output declines. Combined with US exchange inventories unlikely to be re-exported unless LME prices significantly exceed COMEX (currently LME at discount), this dynamic could exacerbate an already-tight ex-US physical market just as the seasonal Q2 draw approaches. records.text: The PBoC has continued to deliver lower fixings, instead of setting a flat fixing or having state banks intervene to curb excessive spot movements. Consequently, we saw a relatively swift, one-way RMB appreciation at the end of the year. We expect the current round of RMB appreciation to continue through January, as exporters’ settlements tend to remain strong until the Chinese New Year. After that, the RMB’s strength is likely to wane, and the exchange rate will become more dependent on external factors, we think. Also, looking back at the RMB appreciation in April–May and August–September 2025, we note that USDRMB tends to trade sideways and stabilize for a while after a short period of relatively rapid appreciation. We expect mild RMB appreciation this year, mainly influenced by USD weakness and US–China rate differential; domestic reflation efforts; export demand and exporters’ settlement demand; the PBoC’s FX policies; and cross-border investment flows. KEY MESSAGES We continue to expect a mild appreciation trend for the RMB, both against the USD and the basket. We see a bumpy downward trend for USDRMB in 2026, with the pair eventually reaching 6.8 at year end. We expect RMB appreciation to be primarily driven by exporters’ higher FX settlement and a weaker USD. But the appreciation is likely to be gradual as we expect domestic deflation to persist, outbound investment to continue and the People’s Bank of China to smooth one-sided FX moves. records.text: Labor Market Stabilization or Jobless Growth? We see the labor market as the most uncertain piece of the 2026 outlook. Our baseline is that a small pickup in GDP growth, a decline in policy uncertainty, and a slower pace of federal government job cuts will boost job growth just enough to stabilize the unemployment rate at 4.5%. But we see the possibility of further softening as the key risk for 2026. Much but not all of the decline in job growth in 2026 reflected a decline in labor supply growth caused by the dramatic decline in immigration. We estimate that the annualized rate of immigration has fallen by about 3mn from its peak over the last two years to just 0.5mn annualized. At that pace we think the economy would need fewer than 70k jobs per month for the unemployment rate to hold steady in 2026, and we see downside risk to even that low number from the increase in arrests by immigration authorities in recent months and from a possible decline in legal immigration this year. Unfortunately, job growth has fallen below even that modest breakeven rate. Our estimate of underlying trend job growth, which combines payroll and household employment and adjusts both for likely data problems, stands at just 11k per month. What is the expected market response to the ruling? If the IEEPA tariffs are overturned, we would expect markets to price in a moderate loss of tariff revenue (so, a wider deficit). That should raise long-end Treasury yields. Stocks are likely to rally on margin relief for retailers and implied fiscal easing. The rally should be more pronounced in sectors that are less vulnerable to Section 232 or 301 investigations (e.g., consumer stocks, as discussed above). Note that the magnitude of the market response would depend on the details of the ruling. For example, will the Fentanyl tariffs also be overturned? Or just the reciprocal tariffs? Will refunds of collected tariffs be mandated? If the tariffs are upheld, we’d expect the opposite outcome: stocks and bond yields lower. The market impact will probably be larger in this direction given that consensus expectation is for the tariffs to be struck down. What is the expected economic impact? We think trade policy will likely be more supportive for growth this year regardless of the Supreme Court ruling. To get a sense of how consensus scores on this front, we use Bloomberg surveys of longer-term (ECFC) eco- nomic projections. In particular, we look at four-quarter- ahead policy rate forecasts, obtaining four observations a year taken at the end of each quarter (only aggregate level fore- casts are available). The quality of Israeli rate predictions is not too different from other low-yielders, but forecast errors are substantial (Figure 4). The consensus systematically over-predicted future hikes in 2010s amid zero-rate policy, and over-predicted cuts in the past couple of years. And the consensus was as wrong on pol- icy amid Covid and war shocks as in other low-yielders. It is possible that the echo of forecast errors of the past several years, when the BoI was more hawkish than anticipated, may be influencing judgments about the pace of the current easing cycle. Interestingly, our analysis suggests that the BoI's own rate projections have slightly lower (absolute) forecast errors compared to the median economist. records.text: K-Shaped Economy Consumer indicators remain mixed. December payrolls was weaker than expected, with growth in employment narrow. UBS Evidence Lab's December Consumer Finances survey suggested that the income outlook for consumers is stable, and cash flow pressures are near average, but more consumers are expecting to miss payments due to job losses. This aligns with the Fed's CES survey noting job loss beliefs worsened and job finding prospects hit a series low. Lastly, consumer loan application data suggests households are embellishing their financial status. We assume a slightly better outlook in early Q1 amid tax refund season if the labor market stabilizes, but these effects will be transitory. This report has been prepared by UBS Securities LLC. The construction underperformance is largely attributable to the government’s austerity drive. Deep spending cuts to secure a fiscal surplus have resulted in the suspension of numerous federal infrastructure projects and a sharp reduction in public investment. records.text: M Idea 12 Lower rates and better earnings trajectory should incentivize borrowers to ramp up capex and spending for business operations. In 2025 we saw very high levels of tech issuance to fund the AI data center demand. While most deals that came to the public credit market were high quality skewed, some deals entered the HY market. We have seen ~$15bn in data center related deals, with most borrowers tapping into HY for the first time. Looking ahead, though not the center of the AI financing eco-system, we do expect the HY market to play a role in AI related financing. We pencil in an increase in AI-related HY supply to ~$20bn, driving the bulk of the increase in GCP volumes that we anticipate in 2026. We have low conviction on this number and see risks skewing to the upside, with AI supply in HY overshooting our target. Institutional Leveraged Loans: $490bn gross issuance (+11% Y/Y) We see continued strong refinancing activity, at $210bn (+8% Y/Y). Refinancing activity slowed in 2025, with total refi volumes coming off the peak in 2024, but was still elevated compared to history. Looking ahead, with additional Fed rate cuts in sight, we see another year of robust refinancing activity in 2026. In particular, there are $59bn of loans due by YE 2027, followed by another $295bn due in 2028, which will come into view. records.text: 9 January 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Week in review As we detailed in our Outlook 2026 report at the end of last year, 2026 is likely to be a year of competing narratives. On one hand we have cyclical resilience, and on the other hand we have structural rigidities. Resilience and rigidity can co-exist for a time. Which one dominates in 2026 will depend on the impact of and interplay between a number of macro factors. This week we have published a series of blogs on those key themes and factors that will likely shape Europe’s macro performance in 2026. These blogs covered fiscal policy and defence spending (blog 1), AI and competitiveness (blog 2), and political uncertainty and inflation (blog 3). Our baseline view is that resilience is likely to dominate in 2026, but unless the rigidities are resolved it will be difficult for the European economy to continue to outperform, at least without generating economic frictions. Headline inflation in the euro area eased to 2.0% YoY in December from 2.1% in November, broadly in line with consensus. The unrounded figure was 1.96%, slightly below our 2.02% forecast. The downside came mainly from core HICP, which fell by a tenth to 2.3% YoY against our expectation of 2.4%. While services inflation was broadly in line with our assumptions (easing to 3.38% from 3.47% in Nov.), core goods inflation was almost 20bps softer than expected at 0.36% YoY – the lowest since Mar-21. records.text: 12 January 2026 UK economic notes Deutsche Bank AG Page 5 taking the annual rate down to -0.2%. We see balanced risks around our forecast. Where to from here? We expect Q4-25 GDP to end up flat. But this will largely depend on any revisions we get to either September or October GDP. We do see a stronger end to the year, however, with December GDP expanding strongly post Budget uncertainty. We will assess our 2025 projections following the November GDP release. Further ahead, as we recently published in our outlook, we remain constructive on the UK economy. Yes, headwinds remain. The labour market remains fragile. Geopolitical uncertainty is rife. But policy is becoming less restrictive and continues to be marginally supportive – at least in the near term with fiscal policy supporting real disposable incomes and monetary policy easing debt servicing costs. Price pressures are also expected to ease meaningfully through the year. And we expect real wage growth to remain steady at around 1%. Overall, we see UK GDP slowing from 1.4% in 2025 to 1.1%, led in large part by negative base effects with quarterly GDP growth projected to average 0.35% q-o-q through the year. See our outlook here. records.text: M Idea 6 Multipolar Friction Continued evolution of multipolar world policy and action remains a key theme for MS globally. The actions by the US in Venezuela brought considered incorporation and extrapolation to the table for investors. Our US public policy team highlight three key considerations for investors at this early stage of developments: US foreign policy shift toward the Western Hemisphere: Recent actions in Venezuela align with the administration’s National Security Strategy and repeated invocation of the Monroe Doctrine, signalling a more assertive US posture in the Western Hemisphere and raising the possibility of further regional interventions. Implications for global and trade policy: This approach fits within the broader shift toward a multipolar world and the “New Washington Consensus,” linking national security with domestic economic interests; it also implies tougher US demands on Mexico in upcoming USMCA negotiations, potential pressure to curb Chinese trade and investment, and the risk of prolonged talks and temporary tariff increases despite a low-tariff zone remaining the base case. Domestic policy and market uncertainty: The focus on executive-driven foreign policy suggests a diminished role for Congress in market-relevant decisions, pointing to elevated political uncertainty and higher risk premia, a dynamic likely to persist into the post- midterms environment, especially under a potential divided government outcome. records.text: The 2025 government shutdown was the longest in history and represented a full lapse in congressional appropriations (in most prior shutdowns, only a few agencies were affected). We expect the shutdown to reduce Q4 GDP growth by 1.1pp, primarily as a result of federal employee furloughs, with a smaller negative effect on federal investment and government purchases (Exhibit 4). The effect will more than reverse in 2026Q1, adding 1.3pp, as furloughed workers return to work and some federal investment and government purchases get pushed from Q4 into Q1. A key point of uncertainty is our net exports assumption. records.text: M Global Idea 2 Cross-Asset Themes We're Watching in 2026 Happy new year to all our readers! To kick the new year off, we think it's worth it to level set – where the roaring rally of 2025 leave us, which markets we are most out-of- consensus on, the major themes we're watching over the next 12 months, and of course how it all drives our cross-asset allocation recommendations. Taking stock – markets had an exceptional year in 2025 2025 was an 'everything rally' year for markets – global equities proxied by MSCI ACWI was up 23% last year, led by Europe in DM and Korea in EM. And even as the US has underperformed other regions, 2025 would mark three consecutive years of 15%+ returns, an extremely rare feat – the only other two times since 1927 that US equities had such a good run were 1995-99 and 2019-21. And fixed income across the spectrum did well too – US AGG and Euro AGG both saw positive total returns, with UST recording the strongest annual performance since 2020. As the cycle shifts gear in 2026, we'll start to see more differentiated performance in the markets, with equities pulling ahead of fixed income: As we've laid out in our 2026 outlook, a supportive policy mix means that investors can shift focus from macro to micro risks, and with AI-related capex acting as a tailwind, risk assets should fare well. records.text: The start of 2026 hasn’t brought a break from the generally low vol end to 2025, but incoming news continues to shape the tilt of risks around rates markets. In the US, having cleared the December jobs report, our forecast for firm early year growth remains a source of upside risk to yields; we favor paying 10s on the 5s10s30s fly. While the broader contours of our outlook appear friendly for carry in the US, we think it pays to be discerning between opportunities. For Europe, 2026 begins with some of our key views continuing to play out in near-term pricing. Despite soggy PMIs, German hard data is improving, with better 2026 growth outweighing longer-term risks to boost Bund yields. And Gilts should benefit both from disinflation and constrained supply, compressing Gilt-Bund spreads and widening Gilt vs OIS swap spreads. Meanwhile, lasting relief in long-end JGB yields hinges on the fiscal picture and may therefore take time, but reduced uncertainty and benign inflation can eventually support long-end absorption and sustain a more balanced outlook. United States and Canada No strong push yet, but cyclical improvement a risk. Progress towards a clear n sense of direction for the US rates market remains slow in the early stages of 2026. On a year-ahead basis we don’t necessarily think that’s wrong, with our baseline that disinflation can aid in global duration digestion and act as a counterweight to better activity, keeping 10y Treasuries rangebound around a 4.2% anchor. records.text: 12 January 2026 FX Blueprint Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Overview It is unlikely that last year's huge drop in the dollar is repeated in 2026. And it is less likely that markets are as dominated by President Trump. Instead, this should be a year where country-specific stories become more relevant. Our big picture starting point remains dollar bearish: the USD has lost its exceptionalism, both as a high- yielder and as a global growth outlier. But our dollar conviction is lower than last year, and we expect EUR/USD to stay range-bound in the first few months of 2026. Growth is the bigger theme in our Blueprint. We prefer currencies with strong domestic recovery stories (AUD, SEK, CZK, ILS) against those where growth is weaker (GBP, CHF, CAD). Large swings in commodity prices are also playing a big role in EM, and we like currencies with high carry and supportive terms of trade (ZAR, BRL, MXN, CLP). From a regional perspective, Asia FX stands out as being extremely cheap. We remain long the yuan, yet also like to sell the yen against it. For dollar weakness to broaden out to the rest of Asia and beyond, the relentless recycling of excess savings into the US needs to show greater signs of turning. In the meantime, we go for growth and attractive yield as 2026 gets underway. Not much excitement in euro, yen in pain We begin the year neutral on EUR/USD, expecting a 1.15-1.20 range for now. To help frame their signaling value, it is helpful to keep in mind that the BLS sampling frame includes both new tenants and continuing tenants, using a sample that is chosen to have characteristics representative of the overall housing stock. By contrast, nearly all the private rent inflation measures track either asking prices or listed rents for new leases. These primarily sample apartments and other high turnover units that are not representative of the overall US universe of rental housing. Most attempt to adjust for rent incentives by looking at effective rents. Most use repeat-rent methodologies that help control for differences in unit characteristics, much as the CPI does. Others (like REIS) do not. As shown in Figure 12, the pace of increase in all of these private measures has declined from pandemic peaks, and all but a few are running below their pre-pandemic run rates on a %y/y basis. Another notable takeaway is that indicators that rely on purely on apartment market data, such as REIS (1.2% y/y) and Apartment List (-0.9% y/y), tend to be running slower than measures that give weight to single-family properties. Notably, the measure of new tenant rents from Figure 3 highlighted by Governor Miran, the Cleveland Fed's New Tenant Repeat-Rent index (NTRR), is an outlier from the general pattern. 12 January 2026 8 Barclays | US Economics

Now imagine that, after a period of time, renters determine that they did not need as much housing as previously thought, so that a portion of the positive demand shock unexpectedly unwinds. Again, the effects of this realization would be felt most acutely in rents for new leases, which would abruptly decelerate to correct the likely overshoot of rents relative to the equilibrium trajectory (Figure 5). Rents for renewal leases would conceivably slow, but not by as much, as there is little or no overshoot to correct. Over time, we would expect market forces to equilibrate rent levels in the two markets, with rents for new leases gradually reaccelerating as this occurs. The agreement was built on their collaboration since 2019 to optimise and industrialise Carbios’ proprietary PET-degrading enzymes and secure enzyme supply for its inaugural industrial-scale biorecycling plant in Longlaville, France. The partnership combines Carbios’ enzymatic technology with Novonesis’ expertise in large-scale enzyme production, enabling near-virgin quality r-PET with lower energy intensity compared to conventional recycling methods and supporting true circularity in PET packaging. Carbios initially planned construction of its enzyme-based PET biorecycling plant in Longlaville in 2023, but the project was postponed due to funding uncertainties and capital cost overruns. However, in its latest press release in December 2025 Carbios said it expects to restart construction of its plant by Q126 (Link). We think that the GSEs will have to stagger their purchases to ensure that any spread tightening has some medium-term durability, or show some willingness to upsize beyond the $200bn. The GSEs have enough non-MBS investments on hand to make most of these purchases, but might also need to issue some debt to maintain a buffer of liquidity for their general operations. The primary rate can be most directly targeted by buying the belly, but there’s also a potential tension with GSE profitability. The GSEs historically have hedged their MBS purchases, meaning that their buying has less of an impact on overall yields and volatility than the Fed’s MBS buying. When GSEs used to buy MBS in size, they did indeed hedge their interest rate risk by shedding duration by paying fixed on swaps, and buying swaptions to offset the negative convexity and vega in the MBS (see Mortgages). records.text: M Idea 2 Activity data point to economic momentum Hard and soft data point toward stronger economic momentum at the end of the year. While the ISM Manufacturing Index pointed toward continued subdued manufacturing output, the sector appears stable and December readings are in line with six-month averages. In contrast, the ISM Services Index improved to 54.4 in December and the employment subcomponent rose 3.1 points to 52.0, the first above-50 reading since May (a month after "Liberation Day"). Elsewhere, the trade deficit surprised to the downside at -$29.4bn in October. In our view, the 3.2% m/m decline in real imports reflects continued payback from the front-loading of imports in 1Q. This is particularly true for consumer goods ex-food and autos, which rose by 148.5% q/q saar in 1Q 25. For exports, nearly all of the rise in October was accounted for by nonmonetary gold, which is not included in GDP estimates since it is considered an asset transfer, not production. That said, the step-up in September exports was less related to trade in nonmonetary gold. Altogether, net trade looks to make another substantial contribution to growth in 4Q. records.text: 's measure of disposable personal income — has receded in recent years to levels that are in line with pre-pandemic norms from 2019. During that year, the ZORI index was rising at an average pace somewhat exceeding 0.3% m/m, or 4% y/y. Housing rental markets do not seem especially loose in comparison to then, with vacancy rates for rental properties now broadly comparable to where they had stood in the leadup to the pandemic (Figure 33). In short, we think risks are weighted toward a tighter housing market and gradually accelerating market rents. As shown in our simulations, CPI rent measures would gradually firm in such scenarios, forestalling the deceleration anticipated by markets. Appendix: Robustness to alternative indicators One could reasonably question our forecast on the basis that ZORI is just one of many indicators, with others showing more pronounced slowing in rents. To consider robustness, we estimate versions of our error-correction specification using quarterly rent estimates from Moody's commercial real estate platform, which the industry commonly refers to as REIS. As noted in our earlier comparison table, this measure reflects effective rents for new and renewed leases for multifamily units in professional-grade properties (mostly apartments). Since such units tend to turn over more frequently than other property types, one could argue that this index provides a better indication of state of the market for new rentals than broader indices such as ZORI. This resilience has combined with tech sector strength to generate above-potential GDP growth and strong profit gains (Figure 1). Sentiment is starting to respond to this development, a point reinforced by this week’s rise in our December composite expectations index. The normalization in sentiment is far from complete, however. Moreover, this week’s activity readings show that a recovery in non-tech business spending and hiring has yet to take hold. Goods producers are expected to reap dividends from a turn away from caution amidst depressed inventory/sales ratios and stagnant non-tech capex. But factory output readings and the latest manufacturing PMI suggest that manufacturers remain stuck in low gear as we turn towards the new year. The subsequent decline is likely attributable to the fact that, as a second-order response, an overly strong euro tends to weigh on equity valuations of predominantly export-oriented European companies (Figure 3). The pickup in equity inflows into Europe is not unique to the EPFR database. It is also consistent with the Eurozone’s balance of payments data, notwithstanding the two-month lag. Already into October, the most-recent available data point, there was evidence of larger inflows into European equities. The historical relationship between such inflows and EURUSD is more mixed, with instances of clear co-movement — such as between 2016-18 — and others of total decoupling, eg, in 2020 and since 2023. Accordingly, the mere presence of equity inflows is no guarantee for EUR outperformance. Global Economics & Strategy12 January 2026ab2 Cross-Asset Views Economic Backdrop UBS key macro forecasts The global economy appears to have held up through Q4, in part because the tariff impact on US inflation and global exports seems further delayed. US policy uncertainty remains high, but outside the US the data are slowly improving, and global confidence is inching higher. records.text: l prices rebounded markedly in July but have largely flatlined since then. But prices of downstream solar panels have not moved much, meaning the transmission has been limited. For the auto industry, the price war shows no signs of easing, with BMW announcing price cuts for about 30 models last week. With the recent CEWC signaling no change in anti- involution stance (see China: Policy meeting continues piecemeal easing path, dated 12 December 2025), we think the authorities are likely to continue with this soft, market-oriented approach in 2026. As a result, we expect the PPI decline to narrow from 2.6% y/yin 2025 to 0.8% y/y in 2026, in no small part due to the improvement in base effect from −1.1pp last year to −0.1pp this year. Two risk factors could facilitate faster reflation this year than our base case envisages: (i) The anti-involution campaign starts to use more forceful measures to curtail production and/or close production capacity. And (ii) stronger imported inflation via a surge in the price of oil or base metals, although, to reiterate, our commodity analysts expect oil prices to decline in 2026 (see the latest Global Outlook). For Treasury Bills (TBs), the MoF has reduced the total issuance of 6- and 12-month TBs from JPY49.2tn in the supplementary budget to JPY40.8tn. Notably, while 12-month T-bills were previously all TBs, the MoF will begin issuing 12-month Financing Bills (FBs), allowing for more flexible adjustment of T-bill maturities. Finally, we anticipate that the MoF will begin issuing T-bill-linked floaters from January 2027, though these were not included in the initial plan. In other words, the MoF may have room to further reduce long and super-long JGB issuance next year. if needed. That could impact hedging and help to dislodge long-held AUD shorts (per the CFTC data), shorts that were trimmed notably as carry crossed the zero threshold (Figure 20). Aussie's beta to global risk sentiment may also have scope to lift from recent levels. Solid global growth in 2026 together with still-elevated inflation risks should favour equities and some commodities. And the profile of commodity rises (that is, excluding oil) may favour AUD expressions more so than other G10 high-betas (like CAD, NOK). Aussie's beta to equity strength may have been softer recently as net equity flows returned to negative as risk appetite improved (Figure 21). Part of that may be structural: AU equity flows are increasingly pointing to a more countercyclical relationship in recent years (Figure 22). But some part may have been exacerbated as Australian pension funds rebuilt global exposures in 2H25 (after a rotation domestically in Q2), and that rebalance should be complete. The upturn in Chinese financial markets has also been a welcome development for AUD, but the transmission to the currency has ultimately been modest in the face of still-declining Chinese infrastructure and real estate. A domestic infrastructure recovery is expected in 2026, and may well be necessary to meet GDP targets amid a still-tepid consumer and the export-constraining effect of a stronger RMB. New inflation trajectory strengthens our view that Banxico will pause easing in Q1: We still expect the central bank will be able to cut its policy rate twice before year end, for a terminal level at 6.5% (see: Banxico’s final cut of 2025 opens the door to a pause, dated 18 Dec). Overall, while headline inflation will remain elevated in early 2026, the broader disinflation process remains intact. In our view, the main implication of recent policy-driven shocks is a delay in the convergence timeline, rather than a change in the destination. In this context, Banxico is likely to adjust its convergence horizon by at least two quarters, currently around Q3 2026, as temporary tax and tariff effects keep headline inflation higher for longer. Importantly, this postponement does not imply a material shift in inflation expectations, as in our baseline, the shocks are largely transitory and have limited spillovers into core dynamics. KEY MESSAGES We are raising our headline inflation forecast for 2026 to 4.0% (from 3.6%), reflecting front-loaded policy- driven price adjustments taking effect in early January. The impact of the excise tax (IEPS) increase should be visible in the first half of January. By contrast, tariff changes are likely to affect inflation more gradually. That said, investors shouldn’t extrapolate too much from this record pace, as in years past the first full week of January is the busiest of the month, and then supply tends to taper down by the 2nd week and continues at a similar pace for the rest of the month ( Figure 8T h e f i r s t w e e k o f J a n u a r y i s u s u a l l y t h e b u s i e s t o f t h e m o n t h ). The last two Januarys have both been at or near record highs ($193bn in 2024 and $190bn in 2025) yet new issues those months tightened by ~2.5bp on the month and also outperformed the index. However, with spreads currently hovering close to record tights, the prospect for new issue outperformance may be more modest. More broadly, in 2025 new issues tightened by 2.5bp on average each month until they entered the index, which was half the 5.3bp of tightening on average in 2022-24. New issues actually widened on average in 4 of the 12 months last year (see Corporates). records.text: discussed in our Year Ahead Report (see Year Ahead 2026: K-shaped economies with K-shaped risks), the US K-shaped economy is one of the most important imbalances to monitor in 2026. Consumption and investment continue outperforming in the US, in line with our more constructive than consensus forecasts. However, consumption dynamics are very uneven across income brackets. The latest Consumer Checkpoint report published by the Bank of America Institute (see: Consumer Checkpoint: Merry but measured) shows that the consumption and income gaps between lower and middle-and higher-income brackets remain significant. Middle and higher- income brackets are spending at a robust pace, while lower income brackets are struggling at the margin. Since lower income brackets represent around 20% of aggregate consumption, we continue observing very robust aggregate consumption dynamics. This gap across income brackets helps explain the decoupling between aggregate consumption and consumer confidence numbers.

The biggest weapon in Japan's arsenal is arguably the GPIF, which holds USD1tn in unhedged foreign assets. Even tactical hedging could act as a powerful signal to the private sector. But we are skeptical the government has much incentive. Yen weakness flatters BoJ and GPIF balance sheets, boosts corporate earnings, and the resulting inflation raises tax revenues. Inflation was arguably a bigger political issue last year: with yen weakness contributing to imported inflation, overtourism, and cost of living pressures - household angst was hurting LDP popularity. However, Takaichi's leadership seems to have changed the script: she is enjoying high approval ratings, helped by her hawkish stance on national security (Figure 9). That arguably reduces the chances of a de-escalation in tensions with China. There is little sign of long-awaited repatriation. Data used in this analysis is available from April 2015 onwards Filtering it down: We exclude factors with little empirical evidence of a sustained risk premium from this universe. This disqualifies our real carry and fundamental trend factors utilising our economic surprise or data strength indices. Our betas to MSCI and to BCOM factors are also shown more for illustrative purposes. The factors display high correlation to the traditional pro-cyclical carry factors in FX, which benefit from a much larger body of fundamental research. Clustering: Beyond this filtering process, a simple correlation analysis suggests the existence of clusters: • Carry cluster with traditional carry, cross-currency basis and cross-sectional skewness. Given the high correlation among these factors, we prefer to consider them as a single driver. We consider this as carry and split the factor equally between these three subfactors. • Cross-sectional and timeseries momentum show limited historical correlation but use the same underlying risk premia. We prefer to allocate risk to a momentum cluster, with equal risk allocation to cross-sectional and timeseries momentum. In the restricted specification, OER accelerates from 0.27% m/m in November to about 0.38% m/m in December, while tenant rents accelerate from 0.13% m/m in November to 0.40% m/m in December.10 Notably, these forecasts are boosted a few basis points by the BLS's mechanical carry-forward imputation implying flat rents in October, which has the effect of widening the rent gap. Thereafter, increases in the two CPI rent measures gradually fade over the course of the medium term, with the extent of slowing varying by scenario. In the base case scenario, both OER and tenant rents decelerate to about 0.27% m/m by end-2027. In the upside case, both CPI rent measures slow to about 0.32% m/m by end-2027, while in the downside case, both slow to about 0.23% m/m. records.text: 20) What if... Europe can reverse the trend on indirect steel imports? Trade protection has been the main discussion point for European steels into 2026; we have been positively surprised by how strong defence measures have been so far for direct steel trade (see Stronger trade measures than expected and Punitive CBAM default values could add to steel and cement inflation for further details). We remain relatively cautious on pricing implications given a still-muted demand outlook, and one of the key risks here is downstream (or upstream) demand diversion. In other words, because the new safeguard replacement quotas and CBAM (for now) don't cover steel-containing goods, this could mean more net indirect imports of steel. This would not be a new trend. Below we show EU steel production vs. net direct steel imports and net indirect steel imports. We define indirect exports as trade in articles of iron/steel, industrial equipment and machinery, and vehicles (including railway locomotives/tracks, aircraft and ships). While the rise in net steel imports is well known (+14mt over the last decade, or ~10% of current annual apparent consumption), we would also flag that indirect steel net imports have increased by 18mt over the same timeframe. This is a combination of Europe importing more downstream equipment from other countries, but also exporting less globally (linked to the loss of international manufacturing competitiveness - driven in part by energy and carbon costs). Extending the horizon into 1H of 2026, we look for positive equity performance, on supportive growth-policy tradeoff, marked by earnings accelerating and broadening, and at the same time inflation that is set to move lower. In particular, inflation could be checked by subdued Brent, softening wage growth and some potential watering down of tariffs. Added to this constructive backdrop is the reducing trade uncertainty, potential improvement in China outlook, higher fiscal spend in Eurozone and continued rapid US AI rollout. Eurozone equities have in the past 3 months broken to fresh highs, and we believe that this will have legs. Further, we are staying bullish on EM and in particular on China equity prospects, looking for 2ndyear of outperformance – stay bullish on Miners, and Cyclicals and Exporters more generally. records.text: The other reason we are confident that inflation will fall further is that two straightforward forces that have driven it lower for three years have a bit further to go. The first is the exhaustion of “catch-up inflation,” where some prices adjust with a longer lag and therefore keep rising at a faster pace until they have caught up. In the most prominent example of this, the shelter category, catch-up ended last year, and the key leading indicator—new lease rent growth—has now fallen to well below its pre-pandemic rate. As a result, we expect the large shelter category to slow from 3.7% to 2.3% by December. The second driver of lower inflation has been labor market rebalancing. Our wage growth tracker has fallen by over 2pp to 3.5%, a rate that is compatible with 2% or sub-2% inflation with productivity growth running near 2%, and survey-based expectations suggest that wage growth has a bit further to fall. This should put additional downward pressure on inflation in labor-intensive non-housing services categories. records.text: 2 1.2 1.1 JOLTS (Jan 7) The November JOLTS report was mixed, with the job open- ings and hires rates both at cycle lows but with the quit and layoff rates improving. Some revisions to hiring and quits in October also make that month look less concerning than it had originally appeared. However, given that unemployment moved up in November while openings fell, the vacancy/ unemployment ratio slipped to a new cycle low, which should help constrain wage growth. The opening rate for October was revised from 4.6% to 4.5% and then declined to 4.3%, tying the cycle low that has been hit a number of times over the past year. Opening rates are flat to down across most industries, though retail trade has shown recent strength. The quits rate had been weakening in tandem with the hires rate, with October originally printing a new cycle low of 1.8%. However, that was revised up to 1.9%, a level seen a number of times over the past year, and the rate then increased to 2.0% in November. Cement pricing steps up a gear in Europe? From January 2026, the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) enters Phase 4 for cement, which entails both a new benchmark, meaning a step down in free allowance allocations, and for these free allocations to start ramping down towards zero by 2034. As such, we expect a meaningful increase in the marginal cost curve, driving structurally higher cement prices. Our analysis reinforces a bullish long-term view on cement pricing and equities. While we expect the impact to be back-end-loaded toward 2030, medium-term pricing should benefit directly from ETS. Based on clinker emissions improvements since the 2016/17 benchmark and recent site closures, we estimate the new benchmark at ~0.65t CO₂/t grey clinker versus 0.693

records.text: o f f e r s w i d e b r e a k e v e n r a n g e s , we present breakeven levels from selling various unhedged straddles. We find the corresponding breakeven levels to be wide with a low probability of yields breaching these levels at option expiry. For instance, selling 3Mx2Y unhedged straddles has a breakeven range of (3.21%, 3.62%) with the spot 2Y yield at 3.45%. We believe that risks to yields are biased to the downside and thus ascribe a low probability of 2Y yields rising 20bp over the coming months. On the other hand, it will require consistently weak data (GDP, labour market, and inflation) for the market to price aggressive easing and thus believe that the bar for a 20bp decline in 2Y yields from current levels is also high. Overall, this suggests that implieds are likely rich. This analysis also suggests that selling 3Mx2Y unhedged straddles (or similar structures) are likely to be profitable over the near-term. Overall, we recommend selling 3Mx2Y gamma with daily delta-hedging (see Trade recommendations). records.text: mited flows The 10s30s EUR swaps curve flattened c.1.5bp today with a focus on PFZW’s life cycle, suggesting investors may have been anticipating a lower allocation to risk free rates for young members in the PFZW life cycle. However, the curve has also been under flattening pressures over the last few weeks already, as Dutch pension fund paying flows have been limited, with a skew towards receiving instead. In the next page, we discuss five potential explanations for that. We continue to forecast that 10s30s can reach c.40- 45bp this year but acknowledge that it can be quite volatile with risks of flattening moves as positioning in steepeners is likely still large. We also expect this Friday a solid labor data, showing that at least the labor market is stabilizing rather than decoupling from spending dynamics. SCOTUS ruling on IEEPA: upside risks to the fiscal deficit In our Year Ahead report, we argued that fiscal policy will be stimulative in 2026, with an estimated fiscal impulse circa 0.4pp of GDP and a fiscal deficit (headline) close to 6% of GDP. This fiscal impulse will be reinforced by easy financial conditions validated by the Fed, though we don’t expect more cuts before the change in the Fed’s leadership. In our forecasts, we penciled in 1.5pp of GDP in terms of revenues from tariffs, assuming 15% effective tariffs, 70% of which comes under IEEPA. In practice, tariff revenues will likely be closer to 1pp of GDP. An adverse SCOTUS ruling on IEEPA this week could trigger a sequence of events that will include replacing those impacted tariffs with new tariffs invoking other sections but on net reducing tariff-related revenues by close to 0.3pp of GDP. Certainly an upside risk to an already quite stretched fiscal deficit given the cyclical position of the US economy.

The sharp share price correction in 2025 has been driven primarily by de-rating rather than earnings deterioration. Year-to-date, 12-month forward EBITDA is down only ~7%, while enterprise value has contracted by ~43%. Looking back to 2022, EV is down ~39%, even as forward EBITDA has increased by ~7%. This pronounced de-rating reflects a significant slowdown in organic gross profit growth, compounded by limited visibility into the business outlook. Organic gross profit growth has been negative through 2023-2025, following exceptional expansion of approximately 50% in 2021–2022. records.text: Outlook for the economy and prices (last updated 28 November) Real GDP contracted in Q3 for the first negative growth in six quarters, reflecting a sharp drop in housing investment and sluggish exports linked to tariffs. However, as the former was driven by institutional factors, we expect a return to positive growth from Q4. Looking ahead, we expect growth of around 1% on average due primarily to firm capital investment on the back of structural factors such as labor-saving expenditures and stable consumption stemming from a recovery in the real income environment under slowing inflation. Although the economic measures decided by the Takaichi administration are limited in terms of their growth-boosting effect relative to scale, they are likely to provide a certain degree of support to the economy. On the price front, we expect CPI inflation excluding perishables (core) to ease as a trend, albeit with fluctuations, in the near term due mainly to declines (y/y base effects) in goods, especially food. However, inflation is increasingly sticky, suggesting any deceleration will be more moderate than we previously expected. Furthermore, services inflation has become increasingly robust as the dynamic synergy between wages and prices strengthens on the back of irreversible structural changes in the labor market. South Africa: positive macro data Narrowing in year fiscal deficit In-year fiscal performance continues to improve. November monthly budget data revealed a deficit of ZAR14.9bn. While this print appears lower than the previous month’s ZAR35.8bn deficit, it is higher than the October 2024 print of a ZAR4.5bn deficit. Tax revenue continues to grow well, at 9.7% year-to-date, while expenditure growth is 5.7% over the same period. As a result, year-to-date the cumulative deficit is tracking ZAR281.4bn versus ZAR306.5bn at the same time last year. At this run rate, we estimate a full year deficit of ZAR321bn, undershooting the National Treasury’s ZAR353bn target for fiscal year ending March 2025.

Macro & Fundamentals: Growth Risks Easing Our economists raised 2026 US real GDP growth to 2.1% (+0.3pp) and forecast a shallower labor market slowdown in H1. Credit-based recession risk has fallen to 23%, driven by stronger corporate profits and improved credit health scores, led by high yield. Offsetting this in part, the timeline for Fed cuts is now expected in Q3, delaying further policy support. Private Credit: Risks Persist But No Near-Term Shock Private credit concerns remain, but the near-term outlook is not deteriorating sharply. Positives include lower leveraged loan default rates into year-end and debt-weighted private bankruptcy filings below average. However, this doesn’t mean that we are out of the woods: distressed ratios ticked higher in December, and count-weighted private filings are still rising. Additionally, sector trends show renewed stress in services and tech even as healthcare filings eased. We expect a modest rise in HY and LL default rates to 1.0% and 2.5%, respectively, for FY26. records.text: ab 12 January 2026 Global Research Global Economics & Strategy Core Convictions (Multi-Asset Rundown) All our views on markets in a single page This 'core conviction' document is our weekly one-page multi-asset rundown where we highlight key events in the week ahead and any view changes (see page 2). Highlights this week We expect Dec core CPI in the US to increase by an above consensus 44bp Tuesday (15bp of which is a reversal of the November report’s downward bias), pushing YoY inflation back up from 2.6% to 2.9%. We also expect strong prints in Jan/Feb and by May core inflation could be running at 3.2%. One factor that could affect our forecast is the Supreme Court’s ruling on the IEEPA tariffs (there had been some expectation of an announcement on Friday), though even if existing tariffs are ruled illegal we expect them to be largely replaced with tariffs under other legal authorities. The US weekly walks through scenarios and their economic impact. We propose a number of new trades in FX on the next page that can perform in different risk scenarios: long USDJPY with an RKO, a dual digital aimed at capturing GBP and EUR strength vs USD, short EURAUD and a short AUDNZD trade. We also like selling rallies in EURSEK and EURNOK. In rates, we remain long US10y and expect spread tightening in US 30y vs SOFR (the announcement that Fannie and Freddie would buy 2% of the outstanding mortgage bonds underlines the administration’s duration focus). We also like receiving ESTR1y in 2y

Given the ongoing divergence between CPI rents and market indicators, we think it is reasonable to question whether the lags at play are more complicated, and more persistent, than markets expect. If so, the notion that shelter inflation would fade to rates resembling benchmarks from market rent indicators may be misguided. The remainder of this piece walks through our thinking on this topic. We begin by setting out an alternative view in which the pace of increase in market rents is a poor benchmark for where CPI rent inflation will eventually settle. This reflects inherent features of the CPI housing sample, including the very large share of rollover leases, that work to mute swings relative to market rent measures. We then build our case by going through details of CPI rent measurement, comparing against features of private rent indicators often used for forecasting. Finally, we show simulations from a modeling approach that helps account for the relative stickiness of the CPI, running through various scenarios that help assess risks around our baseline. records.text: 14 Europe Economic Weekly | 09 January 2026 UK UK Back to School- January 2026 edition Sonali Punhani MLI (UK) sonali.punhani@bofa.com Ruben Segura -Cayuela BofA Europe (Madrid) ruben.segura-cayuela@bofa.com It is time for our customary “back to school” summary. Our base case is unchanged from our Year Ahead outlook (Europe Economic Weekly: Year ahead 2026: Cautiously constructive with risks and lower rates)- We expect 2026 growth at 1.2%, but we tweak the quarterly path and 2027 growth at 1.4%. Inflation is finally likely to reach target in H2 2026 with yearly average of 2.2% and risks to the upside. We expect the BoE to cut twice in 2026 to 3.25% in March/June with risks of a delay/ fewer cuts. Political risks remain and May local elections would be a key test for the premiership of PM Starmer. Sluggish Q4 but we expect recovery thereafter Data for Q4 2025 point to sluggishness and we now expect the economy to stagnate in Q4, weaker than 0.2%q/q expected previously. Recent Conference Board consumer surveys have indicated weaker dining out intentions (link here), and the November survey indicated, "In general, spending trends among consumers this year have increasingly moved towards cheap thrills and necessary services and away from expensive and highly discretionary activities ." The Beige Book covering most November indicated cautious discretionary spending among consumers, particularly those in lower and middle-income tiers (link here). We expect sales at the control group of stores, which feed into the BEA's estimates of goods spending, decelerated to a 0.3% rise in November, after a punchy 0.8% rise in October. The 2025 calendar setup, which matches that of 2014, appeared to indicate a softer September, with some Labor Day sales pulled into August, followed by a stronger October and a more moderate November. records.text: US Economics Weekly9 January 2026 ab 34 US Economics Weekly UBS Research Week Ahead: inflation week We expect an above consensus inflation print next week. We expect the core CPI rose 0.44%, seasonally adjusted, bringing the 12-month core CPI inflation rate up from 2.63% in November to 2.86% in December. The headline CPI likely rose 0.40% in December, and the 12-month rate likely rose just slightly to 2.78% in December from 2.74% in November. We estimate the core CPI monthly change in December to be boosted around 0.15 pp by a partial reversal of the downward bias in the November CPI report. For the headline CPI, we estimate the boost to the monthly change should be around 0.13 pp. We describe the sources of bias in the November report we expect to revert below. Outside of the bias effects, our read of the Adobe Digital Price Index (DPI) for December (which covers items sold online) suggests that the pass-through of tariffs is not complete, but also not accelerating. November PPI and import and export price data will also be due out, rounding out the November PCE prices translation. The BEA confirmed this week that they intend to use an average of BLS’ September and November CPI data for its estimates included in the personal income and outlays report for October. records.text: Based on the meaningful amount of data we already have in hand, we expect another solid increase in consumption growth (+2.4% quarterly annualized) but a decline in residential investment (-5.0%). Our solid consumption forecast reflects three factors. First, strong monthly PCE growth over Q3 significantly lowers the bar for a solid Q4 print, with even no growth in October through December leading to +0.5% quarterly annualized growth due to the high starting level. Second, core retail sales increased 0.8% in October, and healthy Black Friday and Cyber Week spending trends suggest a further increase in November. Third, softer inflation in Q4, which partly reflected the impact of data collection issues that weighed on measured prices in October and November, will boost measured real growth. Our residential investment forecast reflects a large drag from a further slowdown in homebuilding activity based on sharp declines in housing starts since mid-year, including a 4.6% decline in October. Starts have declined as homebuilders continue to respond to the normalizing supply-demand balance, especially for single-family housing. This drag is partially offset by a boost from brokers’ commissions, reflecting healthy existing home sales in October and November, which the November pending home sales report suggested will probably continue. Recycled polyethylene terephthalate (r-PET) refers to PET plastic that has been processed for reuse, typically sourced from beverage bottles and packaging. While traditional recycling relies on mechanical methods that degrade polymer quality over time, modern enzyme-based recycling offers a more sustainable alternative. By using biological catalysts to depolymerise PET into its original monomers under mild conditions, this process delivers near-virgin quality r- PET , consumes less energy than thermal or chemical recycling, and enables true circularity by allowing monomers to be recycled repeatedly without loss of quality. records.text: A Gradual Labour Market Recovery Manufacturing weakness has passed through to the labour market. Manufacturing employment declined by a further 170k (2.3% of manufacturing employment and about 0.4% of total employment) last year. Aggregate employment has remained broadly stable as gains in public administration and social services have compensated for declines in the private sector (Exhibit 4, left). While the brighter economic outlook should lift employment growth, job gains will likely be limited as productivity and hours worked per worker still have a lot of room to catch up relative to their pre-Covid trends. The unemployment rate continued to increase steadily throughout 2025 and currently stands at 3.8%, the highest level since the pandemic (Exhibit 4, right). We expect it to decline gradually starting in 2026 as employment growth slowly picks up and labour force growth slows down owing to an ageing population and lower migration. records.text: the GSEs have historically been relatively active hedgers of their mortgage exposure, which we think would mean that a build in holdings matters more to the behavior than the level of rates. Prior to the GFC, GSE hedging activity was likely a tailwind for rates volatility and contributed to stronger directionality between the level of rates and swap spreads owing to negative convexity-driven swap receiving in rallies or paying in selloffs. The footprint of active MBS convexity hedging is dramatically reduced since then, however. We estimate a $200bn build in mortgage holdings would boost the holdings of active mortgage convexity hedgers by about 25% and could increase paying/receiving flow in a 50bp rally/selloff by ~$20bn in 10y equivalent (assuming the accumulated mortgages are current production; Exhibit 2), incrementally amplifying larger moves. While it’s also possible that the initiation of hedges brings some widening to swap spreads (likely in the belly of the curve), the spread implications would ultimately depend on the instruments used (i.e. swaps and swaptions versus Treasury futures), with heavier use of futures undercutting the initial impact on spreads and/or the extent of spread/rate directionality as rates move. This is closely in line with the 0.29% increase we were previously penciling in. Currently, our forecast corresponds to a 0.25%MoM increase in December core PCE inflation (see below). The clearest evidence of the post-shutdown rebound effect would be in stronger prices for goods like apparel, furniture, or recreation goods. As price collections in November were concentrated in the second half of the month when larger holiday season discounts occur, average prices were likely a bit lower than compared to a usual November. This would lead to softer seasonally adjusted November goods prices. Average prices usually decline further in December, but this decline could be smaller than in a typical year as average November prices were already lower than usual. The dollar faces unique AI concentration risk. The contribution of foreign equity flows in funding America's external deficit is at record highs. This has coincided with the concentration in US market capitalization also sitting at record highs (Figure 3). This mix makes the dollar uniquely exposed to a handful of (AI) companies and by extension more vulnerable to negative tail risks in the sector. With foreign markets offering greater diversification benefits this should further re- enforce the decline of the dollar's attractiveness as a risk-off hedge while making the broader US economic outlook more asymmetrically exposed to a negative AI- tail. Fed pricing leans a little too dovish. The biggest bullish risk to the USD in coming months is Fed pricing. US real rates have already declined significantly but rate pricing is the most dovish in G10 markets, leaving the market vulnerable to a hawkish repricing if the labour market stabilizes (Figure 4). records.text: und investments. We continue to see export to be the main source of cross-border inflows. We expect China’s exports will continue to grow in 2026 albeit at a moderated pace (see Link to Jac’s latest piece). We expect outbound investments to continue, especially to EU and EM countries, to facilitate trade re-routing. Meanwhile, ODIs should encourage locals to use the RMB more as a financing currency, thereby supporting the goal of RMB internationalization. We think China will continue to expand portfolio investment to Hong Kong, incentivized by China’s policy support (see China: Further expansion of outbound investment tools, dated 10 July 2025). Mainland Chinese investors net-bought more than USD180bn of HK-listed equities in 2025, a 74% increase from the previous record of USD104bn in 2024. That said, we do expect foreign inflows to return to China onshore equity market as we expect the ‘slow bull’ to maintain in 2026, which could offset some of the portfolio outflows (see Tracking China’s capital market reforms: CSI A500 ETFs see strong December inflows, dated 5 January 2026). Foreigners, however, are still unwinding previously accumulated China bond ASW positions. The launch of cross-boundary bond repo is an effort to re-engage foreign interests in China bonds in exchange for RMB liquidity given the cheap RMB funding costs. However, we believe that Chinese bond yields may need to recover further before foreign investors return as the hedging costs also edged higher on RMB

records.text: channels through which technological change can create new n kinds of jobs. First, it can create new occupations directly. More than 6mn workers are currently employed in computer-related occupations that did not exist 30-40 years ago, while another 8-9mn are employed in roles enabled by the gig economy, e-commerce, content creation, or video games. Second, it can create new occupations by enabling increased specialization. Third, it can indirectly boost discretionary demand in occupations that emerge due to income gains, even if these roles were already technologically feasible. For example, 1mn workers today are employed in pet care, nail salons, educational support/tutoring, and athletic coaching occupations that emerged over the last 30 years. Even under our optimistic assessment that AI will create new jobs, we anticipate n an increase in frictional unemployment as workers transition to new jobs. This implies the momentum of growth is strengthening from +1.0% in FY2025 to +1.2% in FY2026. The economic outlook for 2026 is positive, supported by three tailwinds. First, the global economic outlook is favorable. On a global scale, it is reasonable to assume that the current momentum in AI-related investments is unlikely to fall anytime soon while fiscal policies are supportive for major economies. Second, on the domestic front, real wages are finally expected to turn positive as suggested from a BoJ survey on firms stances on wage growth and an expected fall in inflation. Third, fiscal policy is expansionary, suggesting CY2026 expenditures rising by one percentage point of GDP . That said, downside risks persist from Japan-China tensions, fiscal sustainability concerns, and pessimism over demographic trends. Knowing who will buy the supply has little meaning in the absence of knowing the timing and price at which those purchases occur. • What determines timing and price at which investors make the decision whether to buy, hold, or sell? More often than not, the answer comes back to the macro environment and its impact on central bank decision making. In the absence of knowing who will buy, when, and at what price, how should investors think about supply and its impact on price? We discuss the impact of supply on price in Between a Rock and a Hard Place. In short, sovereign supply moves market prices the most when expectations form or change from previous expectations for sovereign supply. • In 2026, surprises to the outlook for fiscal policy seem most likely to change expectations for the sovereign supply outlook. • This means that bond yields can fall (rise) if investors come to expect less (more) supply than they thought before – even if that supply is more (less) than what they had to buy previously.

Federal Reserve Commentary FOMC call change: A matter of timing Following a reduction in the unemployment rate to 4.4% in December and with inflation prints expected to be elevated in coming months, we delay our projected 25bp rate cuts to June and December. We then expect the FOMC to maintain rates at 3.00-3.25%. Delaying our rate cut projections to June and December With the latest job estimates downplaying downside risks to the labor market that would justify additional risk management cuts, we are adjusting our rate call. We now expect 25bp cuts in June and December 2026, both premised upon the FOMC seeing hard evidence that inflation is diminishing toward its 2% target over the course of next year. With data on activity looking fairly solid and measures of spending and activity exceeding expectations in late 2025, we think the window for additional risk management cuts may have closed. We were already expecting a pause at the January meeting, with the FOMC taking time to assess the effects of recent rate cuts. However, we previously projected that the next rate cuts would take place in March and June. This was based on the expectation that the FOMC would remain concerned about deteriorating labor market conditions and the assumption that the it would see evidence that tariff-led price increases have peaked, on a m/m basis, thereby gaining confidence that inflation would return toward the 2%

Political resistance to rate hikes remains a risk, and while not our baseline, a sharper-than-expected US labor market slowdown could disrupt the near-term normalization path. Moreover, anecdotal evidence points to concerns around the adverse impact of China’s export controls on the Japanese economy as well as rising global geopolitical tensions. These risks cannot be fully ignored, and recent highs in 1y1y or 2y1y likely reflect the market being priced for near-term perfection, in our view. Relatedly, we have emphasized the importance of cross-market developments in 2026, both through the FX and rate channels. In this context, repriced expectations for an early hike in Australia were marginally supportive of JPY rates, in our view. Our read of the Adobe Digital Price Index (DPI) for December (which covers items sold online) suggests that the pass-through of tariffs is not complete, but also not accelerating. After slowing in November, the 12-month price change for the Adobe DPI rose in the December update, but remains a bit below the recent peak in September and October. Twelve-month inflation also rose in 13 of the 18 Adobe DPI categories. The step down in used car prices should be temporary, as the weakness in wholesale used vehicle prices appears to have passed and new car prices are rising. Why we are bullish on Novonesis: multiple growth engines drive structural upside In our view, Novonesis is uniquely positioned to deliver sustained growth thanks to a diversified set of engines. Bioenergy has transformed from a volatile segment into a structural growth driver, now contributing ~17% of group revenue versus 12% in 2021, supported by innovation and geographic expansion beyond the US, into Brazil and India. India stands out with ethanol blending targets and policy support driving ~40% volume CAGR since 2020, alongside a shift to grain-based feedstock and second-generation (2G) ethanol, which significantly boosts enzyme penetration. We expect India and Brazil to continue to drive the growth, with increased penetration in 2G (which requires 10x more enzymes than 1G) and an increased blending mandate (Brazil recently increased its mandated blending requirement). Novonesis’ Household Care segment is structurally positioned for mid-single-digit growth, with the the company expect market to normalise at 1–3% over the cycle. We believe the company is well placed to outpace the broader market through innovation-led solutions and regional penetration, particularly in emerging markets such as India. records.text: M Idea 2 Autos boost headline sales, moderation in retail control We expect that headline retail sales were boosted by auto sales in November, and rose by 0.4% m/m, and headline ex-autos rose 0.3% m/m. Retail control, however, shows some payback from the outsized growth in October, and rises by 0.2% m/m. The factors that push our forecast for control into this lower estimate are: slower growth in nominal labor market income in November, lingering effects from the federal government shutdown, softness in prices of goods ex-autos. There was also broad weakness in November credit card transactions data, with negative m/m prints across most spending across categories (which was largely reversed in the December transactions data). Among the other components, auto unit sales grew at a solid pace in November, and given the strength in new car prices, we expect auto sales were up +1.1% m/m. Sales at gas stations are expected to increase by 1.9% given the strength in gas prices. We expect another month of decline in restaurant sales, -0.2% m/m. We expect building material sales were flat in November after the weak September and October. We recently revised our real consumption spending forecast upwards on the back of the momentum in the delayed incoming economic data and the softness in October/ November prices. According to the German chemical association, Verband der Chemischen Industrie (VCI), order intake by year-end was 20% below pre-crisis levels, with one in ten companies saying they now plan to close entire locations, and more than 40% expecting sales to fall again in 2026. After an estimated 3% drop in chemical industry sales in 2025, VCI now forecasts an even steeper decline of 3.5% in 2026. Against this backdrop, the key question is which companies are best positioned to weather the storm - and whether consistent dividend payers in the sector could be at risk in the upcoming year. While dividend yields in the diversified chemicals space appear attractive at first glance (as high as 9% for names like Evonik and Solvay), they increasingly reflect market scepticism over sustainability. It is therefore crucial to assess where the true risk- reward balances lies - distinguishing between companies that can maintain resilience and those where yields may signal justified elevated risk. Overall, despite structural headwinds in the sector, we do see a tactical opportunity for investors with a 6- to 12- month horizon to lock in high headline yields in scenarios where dividends are not cut. records.text: Cayla Seder, Marvin Loh January 9, 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Classification: Complimentary Material Fund Connect Quarterly: I spy neutral Monetary policy is entering 2026 in a similar fashion to how it started last year. Mainly, the Fed is once again expected to remain on an extended hold after executing a series of rate cuts at the end of the prior year. And while inflation uncertainty remains a primary driver of this reticence, most of the similarities stop there. Unlike last year, investors were much more concerned about growth, with 40% odds of a much more aggressive Fed, versus just ½ that now. Additionally, while disinflation continues, the December payrolls report shows that wage pressures are building, rather than easing. Why confidence in cuts then? We suspect that the expected changing of the guard is coming into play. With Powell’s tenure as chair down to just 3-meetings, there is little reason to think that his replacement will not try to at least get to neutral more aggressively. So for the moment, we remain rangebound, subject to data, which should keep volatility suppressed until we get more cl arity on disinflation, strong growth and the priorities of incoming Fed leadership. LANDING THE PLANE: With the most recent 25bp cut to 3.50–3.75% in December, the FOMC has moved into the upper bound of what is generally viewed as the neutral range. As a result, the bar for additional easing is now higher, particularly given the divided views on

The widespread failure of Asian currencies to rally last year, despite in certain cases holding the largest amount of US assets to hedge, was a puzzle. The sharp rally in equity markets to start 2026 is another positive. Asian currencies have notably lagged what is a typically important driver for the complex (Figure 45). A missing ingredient for a rally is central bank policy helping to narrow interest rate differentials with the US but in certain countries the market has already shifted towards pricing hikes after a synchronised easing cycle across the region last year. EM monetary policy remains highly credible. EM central banks were largely comfortable with lagging the Fed when it came to monetary policy easing last year (of the core central banks in CEEMEA and LatAm only Banxico and CBT delivered more than the Fed's 75bp cuts). records.text: We expect business investment to be the strongest component of GDP in 2026, growing 5½% Q4/Q4. Business investment should benefit from easier financial conditions, reduced policy uncertainty, and more generous tax incentives. At the industry level, tax policy changes from the OBBBA should reduce the cost of capital and boost investment most in the manufacturing sector, though its impact there will be offset by the fading effect of Inflation Reduction Act and CHIPS Act subsidies. We expect investment in artificial intelligence to contribute about 1.5pp to measured capex growth this year, but the net impact on GDP growth would be only 0.1-0.2pp because much of the spending will be on imported equipment. Residential investment is likely to remain weak in 2026 for familiar reasons: mortgage rates remain high, affordability is constraining demand for single-family housing, a great deal of new apartment supply has come online in recent years or is nearing completion, and lower immigration is a hit to both the demand and supply sides. As we've noted elsewhere, prior to 2000, government bond yields have gone up during large equity sell- offs and did not see any gains which offset equity losses. Current correlations are not significantly far from stock-bond correlations through the 1990s, when – like today – growth was also solid and technology diffusion was driving productivity gains. Services components such as packaged holidays (mainly in Germany and Spain) were the main driver – excluding those, m/m SA core inflation was well below target (Exhibit 7). Low-contact services, the less volatile part of services, continued to show some timid signs of disinflation (Exhibit 12).
